speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a motion of some urgency to move under the provisions of Standing Order 43. It will be of interest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and, I hope, the whole House generally.
While recognizing the need for the government to prevent foreign flag ships from taking advantage of the low domestic price for fuel in Canada, this policy has, as the minister is aware, singled out DMA members who are registered Canadian companies as the lone segment of Canadian industry required to pay world fuel prices for international trade. This will result in an additional $30 million in costs, encouraging our shippers to use less fuel-efficient modes of transport and having a detrimental impact particularly on the Quebec-
Labrador mining industry, as well as forcing grain cargo route diversions.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ADVANCE NOTICE OF COMPANY MERGERS- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. There has been a rapidly increasing number of mergers going on within the Canadian economy. It was in the order of one thousand over the last three years. That is grossly underestimated in terms of the assets and the numbers involved, because the government obtains its information only by clipping files out of the newspapers. This country more and more is beginning to resemble a banana republic in which the economy is concentrated in the hands of a small number of families, such as the Bronfmans, the Irvings, the Westons, and so forth.
I move:
That the minister urge the government to pass regulations requiring any person wishing to proceed with a merger or takeover of a Canadian business to give the government written notice in advance of his intentions in these matters.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS IN ANNUAL REPORT RESPECTING GOVERNMENT POLICIES
speechtext: The annual report of the Bank of Canada for 1980 was made public yesterday. It reviews the experience of the last five years in fighting inflation in Canada and concludes by saying "we have made only limited progress". The report concludes that the lack of success was not due to the fact that the government's anti-inflationary fiscal or financial policies were ill conceived, but rather because they were pursued with gradualism. My question to the minister is this. The bank says it will continue these policies, which will mean high interest rates and tight money over the next five years, presumably with his approval. Likely this will mean that inflation and high interest rates will continue, unless there is a new fiscal approach by the government, because until now the minister's approach has been one of gradualism. Will the minister adopt a new fiscal approach to correspond with the approach of the Bank of Canada and, if so, what will that approach be?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS IN ANNUAL REPORT RESPECTING GOVERNMENT POLICIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if I understood the comments of the Governor of the Bank of Canada when he spoke about gradualism, he was speaking about the application of monetary policy. I would draw to the attention of the hon. member that the governor himself said in his annual report that he was pleased that in the last budget the government recognized the need to reduce its over-all deficit in the years ahead. subsubtopic: STATEMENTS IN ANNUAL REPORT RESPECTING GOVERNMENT POLICIES

In view of the reports which claim, to no one's surprise in the New Democratic Party, that the Canadian public is paying some $56 million extra for health care than they should be, as a result of extra billing, can the minister tell us whether she is now prepared to bring in amendments to the Medical Care Act as recommended by Mr. Justice Hall, to ban extra billing before a bad situation becomes worse and medicare, as we have come to know it, goes down the drain?

I am pleased to have a chance to state very clearly our position on extra billing. It is no news to Canadians that this government is opposed to any form of extra billing. If the federal government were to ban extra billing right away, it might easily be challenged in the courts,

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Dartmouth-Halifax East) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION PROBLEMS
speechtext:
That this House condemns the failure of the government to deal adequately with national transportation problems, and specifically condemns the Minister of Transport for:
1.	abandoning the use of transportation as a tool of national and regional economic development;
2.	allowing Canadian National Railways to totally disregard legitimate maritime business needs and close CN Express offices without adequate financial justification;
3.	permitting CN Marine to impose excessive increases in ferry rates for 1981 after showing an $8 million profit last year;
4.	failing to ensure an adequate supply of reefer cars or to recognize the growing requirement for farm door "piggy back" trailer service, particularly in Prince Edward Island;
5.	failing to initiate changes designed to speed up the "appeal" system under the CTC regulatory process, causing substantial dollar losses to Atlantic transportation users;
6.	allowing a serious deterioration in freight rate structures, leading to a loss of the traditional parity between river and coastal ports;
7.	failing to bring before the House acceptable legislation dealing with a new national transportation act, ports policy, the Maritime Code, or coastal shipping;
8.	permitting unconscionable delays in providing a new air terminal in Charlottetown; and
9.	allowing undue delays in the construction of the St. John's syncro-lift facility.
He said: Madam Speaker, part of the purpose of my motion today is to try to bring to the attention of government supporters opposite some of the very pressing and historic problems that Atlantic Canadians face in the area of general transportation. Earlier this afternoon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) indicated to the House that as time goes by transportation is becoming less and less important to people in Atlantic Canada. Well, obviously the minister was speaking on the advice of others, not from any personal knowledge, or he would never have made that comment, particularly in the context in which he made it.
For over 115 years the central government has caused problems in this area, to the serious economic, social and cultural disadvantage of the people of Atlantic Canada. The suggestion that everything is fine there with respect to transportation, that it is going along great and that we do not consider it a problem, is utter nonsense and should be rejected out of hand.
My motion, Mr. Speaker, ranges from freight rate structures to the fiasco involving the syncro-lift facility in the port of St. John's. We have seen the abandonment by CN of the rail line along Nova Scotia's eastern shore at a point in time when that province had just started construction of an industrial park based on the presence of that rail line. We have witnessed inexplicable delays in the construction of a new air terminal at Charlottetown, in the works for five years. We learned today it is another two to three years down the road. It was promised five years ago! We are now looking at a seven-year fiasco.
There has been continued procrastination by this government with respect to the gradual redevelopment of the Canadian deep sea fleet. There has been a thoughtless approach in implementing fuel surcharges. 1 just raised this subject with hon. members on the treasury benches. Surcharges on shipping fuel lump foreign and Canadian ships into one discriminatory basket. There are a dozen and one other very clear examples which we will attempt this afternoon to bring forcibly to the minister's attention. There continue to be marine transportation and general transportation problems for us in Atlantic Canada.
The motion cites nine basic reasons. We talk firstly about abandoning the use of transportation as a deliberate tool of national and regional economic development. For years Treasury Board officials and former ministers of transport right up to the last minister of transport committed themselves to the deliberate use of transport as a tool of development, but government, if for no other reason than the three or four examples I cited just a moment ago, has in fact not used transport as a tool of development.
There are contradictions. The left hand does not know what the right hand is doing. Facilities have been built; federal assistance has been sought; there has been some degree of approval; but then the Ministry of Transport allows Canadian National to tear up lines intended to service the industrial sector. We are not deliberately using transport as a tool, when it could be the most useful tool we have available to us.
We have allowed Canadian National Railways to disregard totally legitimate maritime business needs. CN Express offices have been closed without adequate financial justification. The
March 17, 1981

Standing Committee on Transport dealt with this issue some weeTcs ago. Just a number of days ago the report of the Standing Committee on Transport was concurred in by the House of Commons. That report called on the minister to use his offices to direct Canadian National to maintain express service at the 1979 level. We hope that during the course of the debate this afternoon the Minister of Transport or others on his side of the House who speak will be pleased to indicate to us just how the minister intends to react to that direct request of this House. Will he accede to the wishes of the House, or will he ignore them? We will be interested in hearing about that later on.
With respect to CN Marine ferry rates, we understand there is a proposition before the government which would reorder the terms of reference within which CN Marine and the regulatory agencies arrive at formulae for increasing rates. This will be dealt with in greater depth by one of my colleagues later on. However, we wonder what the minister will have to say about putting in place new terms of reference and setting new directions with respect to CN Marine ferry rates. That august agency made for itself $8 million or $10 million profit last year.
In our motion we have touched on the historic numeric inadequacies of reefer cars for potato producers in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. In the 15 or 16 years I have been in this House I have not once gone through a year in which western grain producers were not howling about boxcars and hopper cars. Over that same period Atlantic potato producers and other horticultural producers experienced the same desperate need for reefer cars and other means to get their produce to market. This is what we are concerned about. The problem is chronic, and it is real. The minister suggests that it is other than that, but that merely indicates to the people of Atlantic Canada that he has not bothered to take a close look at this himself.
Some years ago there was a movement on the part of the government to examine closely the Canadian Transport Commission, which regulates transportation. Out of that came some thoughts about breaking down the CTC and establishing in western Canada a regional office which would give western producers and western transportation people geographically and psychologically closer access to their regulatory agency, the CTC. When the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski) became minister of transport, he picked that idea up and carried the ball. There now is in operation in western Canada a branch office, so to speak, of the CTC.
Aside from the generally beneficial effect of decentralization in these matters, the purpose of the CTC is to reflect realities and respond more adequately to the needs of Canada's regions. Westerners no longer have to deal with Ottawa either in terms of geography or the psychology which comes about with respect to distance every time they need new licences, renewals or rulings or every time they wish to state grievances regarding rulings. But lo and behold, not only do we in Atlantic Canada not yet have this facility; there is no indica-
Transportation
tion we will ever get it. That is again another prime example of ignoring the legitimate needs of eastern Canadians.
There should be established in eastern Canada an office of that regulatory agency which is accessible to eastern users of transport and those directly involved in transportation as an industry. The delay is inexcusable. Eastern Canada should be treated at least on an equal basis. There should also be the recognition that, like Ontarians and Quebecers, we too are Canadians.
We have taken a run at the minister for something which is historical and runs a little deeper than some of us in Atlantic Canada care to see continue happening. It is manifested by the apparent deterioration in the competitive position of eastern producers as a result of inadequate control and monitoring of freight rate structures. There is developing in eastern Canada a growing sense of mistrust of Canadian National Railways. CN is our lifeblood. God knows that except for the port of Saint John all of us are captive to the CN. We know what the CN has done in recent years in relation to general freight rate structures. We know its attitude with respect to the closing of its express offices. We know about its involvement in CAST, which is the most damnable involvement any minister of transport could permit of a Crown agency. Crown agencies must act in contemplation of good business practices and in contemplation of profit.

speechtext:
However, that should not lead to a growing appearance of conflict of interest which Canadian National is beginning to enjoy now in the eyes of Atlantic Canadians. There may not be conflict of interest today, nor was there four or five years ago when the minister's predecessor once removed allowed Canadian National to involve itself in CAST steamships, but that potential conflict of interest is rearing its ugly head in the port of Halifax today. I suggest to the minister that he is not so naive as not to know that there is some grain of truth in what I am saying and some reason for me and others on the east coast to worry. At some point in the not too distant future, that conflict of interest could result in a disastrous rate war between shipping lines servicing the ports of Halifax, Nova Scotia, and Saint John, New Brunswick, and shipping lines servicing ports from Quebec City to Montreal. We condemn the minister for having allowed this to happen.
The former minister of transport, the hon. member for Vegreville, did much in his short time in office to correct and stem this disastrous trend. In the past, the minister has not seen fit to pick up and carry on where his predecessor left off. They were good programs, the programs I mentioned. I say to the minister: give us an eastern office of the Canadian Transport Commission. It was a good idea, and let him not reject it just because it came from this side of the chamber. If it is a good idea, let him use it. We welcome the positive and beneficial initiatives of the Minister of Transport and his colleagues on the treasury benches.

March 17, 1981
Transportation
I will give an example of that, Mr. Speaker. A prime example is the Ocean Industries agreement which has been ready for signature for over a year. Where is it now? It is not in the office of the responsible minister, not in the Treasury Board nor in cabinet. It sits on the desk of the political minister for Nova Scotia, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen). And why will he not approve it? He will not approve it because the minister of industry and development in the province of Nova Scotia said to a reporter one day: "The details of the agreement are included, and we have agreement". That was months and months ago. The Deputy Prime Minister said to himself: "I will teach that whipper-snapper a lesson; you people in Nova Scotia will not get your Ocean Industries agreement until I am ready to approve it". I wish that distinguished Cape Bretoner were in the House because I would like to say to his face that we do not appreciate that. That is just an example, and I will not dwell on it any further.
How have all these things happened? We could go on and on about this if the minister would listen this afternoon. Probably it has happened because the present National Transportation Act in this country is 14 years old. It reflects the thinking of 15, 1.6, 18 years ago. In the early 1960s we were drafting the act which ostensibly governs the development of transportation policies in this country. The transportation policy dreamt up and prepared in the early 1960s does not adequately meet the demands of that sector in the 1980s; it is long past due.
When will the minister and the government address themselves to the problems of putting a clear statement of philosophy and principle in front of the Canadian people from which can flow the essential transportation policy and legislation which is required to sort out the mess in transportation, not only in eastern Canada but in Canada generally? I think probably that is at the root: we have no philosophy to which we can attune a port policy or a coastal shipping policy. We have no standard against which we can measure the desirability of the gradual development of a Canadian deep sea fleet, although failure to do so is costing us about $4 billion annually. We have no statement from this government, nor have we had a statement from any government for some 12 or 14 years now, on what the essence of transport and transport legislation is and should be in this country. In front of us we have 15 or 20 carts, but we do not have a horse to push them-the old one is 12 or 14 years now and he was put out to pasture two or three ministers of transport ago.
Nobody, apart from the former minister of transport, has given any public indication of the desirability and necessity of bringing forward a new National Transportation Act. We need a new act. We need a new ports policy, and we need to complete the five books of the Maritime Code. We have to resolve the coastal shipping program. We have to resolve the fuel surcharge problem or we will drive users of water-borne vehicles, the most efficient mode of transport, to using less efficient modes of transport which do not have to pay the surcharge, which is discriminatory in itself.
I referred to the air terminal at Charlottetown. It was somewhat alarming for us to learn earlier today that a st'udy, which we thought had been completed in the minister's department some months ago, is just now at the point where yet a further study can be undertaken with respect to the provision of new air terminal facilities at Charlottetown. We learned quite by accident earlier today-although probably it had been known-that in place of a new air terminal they are going to add 15 feet on to the luggage handling section of the airport at Charlottetown right on the eve of the 1981 tourist season in that province. It is mind boggling!
The purpose of today's debate is to draw to the attention of the minister and his parliamentary secretary-both of whom we are very pleased to see in the chamber-as well as the other members of the Standing Committee on Transport, selected topics, by no means all-inclusive, and examples of the concerns of transportation users in Atlantic Canada.
I have not even touched upon rail passenger service, the difficulties at the Halifax International Airport or the continuing difficulties with air connections in and out of Fredericton, New Brunswick. I have not talked about the regional air carrier policy or the need for much closer, effective working arrangements between Air Canada and the regional air carrier. The list is somewhat exhaustive.
Over the course of the next two or three hours, the House will hear from my colleagues from St. John's West, Malpeque, Carleton-Charlotte, Hillsborough and Annapolis Valley-Hants about these and other problems which confront the people of Atlantic Canada.
I close by reiterating my concern that some ministerial adviser got to the Minister of Transport and said to him: "Do not worry about transport in Atlantic Canada; our best advice to you is that they no longer consider it important". As long as this government is in office, I do not ever expect to know one Atlantic Canadian who will not, at the drop of a hat, give me 101 reasons why the government should resign or 1,001 reasons why the Minister of Transport should resign.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate. Transportation in Canada needs much more attention than it has been receiving. At the outset I want to say that we have carefully read the motion of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) on behalf of the official opposition and we agree with the motion proposed by the hon. member.
His motion starts off by condemning the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) for abandoning the use of transportation as a tool of national and regional economic development. We agree that a national transportation policy should be used as an active instrument to encourage regional growth, but successive federal governments have not done this. Instead, they have treated transportation in isolation.
March 17, 1981

Prior to confederation, Atlantic Canada had a prosperous trade up and down the east coast of the United States. When it was decided to develop Canada as a country independent of the United States, confederation encouraged east-west trade by building the Intercolonial railway. Thus, the deal was a national policy of relatively low-cost east-west transportation to the maritimes and protection of central Canadian industry. Now the problem is that Atlantic Canada is not provided with low-cost, efficient east-west transportation. This situation must be changed if our country is to grow stronger, particularly in Atlantic Canada. Poor east-west transportation will continue to balkanize our regions and encourage them to do more north-south trade because transportation costs may be cheaper or more convenient.
The second paragraph of the motion condemns the minister for allowing CN Express to pull out of Atlantic Canada as well as other parts of the country. I thank the members of the Standing Committee on Transport from both the other parties for supporting my motion to which the House unanimously agreed last week. How can the minister and his government accept a motion which asks the government to consider doing a certain thing regarding CN Express and not take some action on it? He cannot use the excuse that CN must make these corporate decisions independently. I could recite a motion which was accepted in the House in 1970 or 1971 on CN pensions which CN chose to ignore. The minister of that day got in touch with CN and let them know that they had darned well better do it. He can do the same thing now.
Point three condemns the minister for allowing CN Marine to impose ferry rate increases. We believe that the national government, in concert with the provinces, should treat our ferries and coastal services as an integral part of our rail and highway systems. There should be nominal tolls and, in some instances, there should be no tolls. Certainly there should be no increases. They should be funded as our highway systems are funded. At least 21 new vessels should be built for ferry and coastal services for Atlantic Canada alone.
The fourth point condemns the record on potato movement. Since 1968 the transport committee was in Atlantic Canada three times, and the same problem was presented on every occasion; there is nothing new about it. It is not only the supply of reefer cars for potato movement; the railroads have never provided sufficient accommodation to handle the traffic in almost every commodity for shipment out of Atlantic Canada, western Canada and some parts of central Canada, as is required under Section 262 of the Railway Act. There is a shortage of stock cars, cars to move fruit and vegetables, cars to move potatoes, cars to move grain and so on.
The fifth point condemns the slow appeal system of the CTC. We agree that the Railway Act and the National Transportation Act should be amended to protect shippers and to speed up the process.
Point six condemns the freight rate structures. A railway consultant recently said that CN rates on containers are double the cost of providing service. In fact, the consultant said that CN could cut its rate on containers from Halifax to
Transportation
Montreal by half and still make a profit. Those high costs hurt maritime ports.
The entire matter of rates has been a chronic problem in Atlantic Canada as well as western Canada. There are still anomalies which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and previous ministers of transport agreed should be corrected. For example, in 1977 it cost 2.8 cents per tonne mile to haul fish 800 miles from central Canada to Atlantic Canada, but it cost nearly double that amount, or 5.29 cents per tonne mile to haul fish from Atlantic Canada to central Canada. There are problems with the steel industry in Cape Breton. In 1979 it cost 71 cents per hundred pounds to ship steel billets 375 miles from Hamilton to montreal, but it cost $2.84 to ship a hundred pounds of steel billets 354 miles from Sydney to Moncton. Nothing has been done about those rate anomalies, to put it mildly.
The seventh point condemns the minister for his failure to bring in amendments to the National Transportation Act, the Maritime Code or bring in a policy on coastal shipping. The National Transportation Act should be amended to give regional development priority over profits. The shipping legislation needs to be updated. The hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) will deal with that later. The Minister of Transport has implemented a new ports policy without consulting Parliament. He approved Treasury Board action which forgave interest payments on $300 million of National Harbours Board debt but opposed the marching orders from Ottawa that all NHB ports are on their own and must be profitable.
I was glad to see the change of heart by the official opposition. On September 26, 1979, the then minister of transport had his National Harbours Board chairman telex every port commissioner in Canada asking for a business plan which would make each port self-financing within three years. The telex read:
Would you please review all of your port's tariffs and submit a plan for proposed increases up to 1982, which will result in revenues equal to or greater than-
He was referring to the cost of operating the ports. I am glad that there has been a change of heart since in Halifax there has been, for example, a 400 per cent increase in rental fees per square foot used for containers. No wonder containers go to Montreal instead of Halifax. It is the principle of user-pay; the port must break even or make a profit.
The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East mentioned the delay in building a new air terminal at Charlottetown. I want to tell him that we fully agree and sympathize with him over that delay. But he should take a look at what has been happening in Regina-or, rather, what has not been happening in Regina. Five years ago the deputy minister of air administration told me in the transport committee that the construction of an air terminal in Regina would be completed within three years. That was five years ago and it has not even been started yet. In fact, plans are being drawn again and the

March 17, 1981
Transportation
time-frame for completion is now 1985 or 1986. We outgrew our airport terminal about eight or ten years ago. So, the situation is not just peculiar to Charlottetown. I submit that places like Regina, St. John's and Moncton are in a similar category.
There has been no action on the synchrolift facility at St. John's. The construction of that facility would add 150 jobs to that shipyard and would increase its capacity.

speechtext: Two hundred jobs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION PROBLEMS
speechtext:
The hon. member says 200 jobs, which is all the better. The capacity of every shipyard in Canada should be increased. Government should adopt a policy to create a Canadian merchant marine and encourage Canadian shipbuilding.
The motion presented by the official opposition today, Mr. Speaker, is one that we can support. We want to add three more points to it which we believe will be acceptable to my colleagues to my right and, hopefully, to the government.
I suppose that the motion is somewhat hard on the present minister. At the moment I am not about to ask him for his resignation, although if he will clean up his act and implement a large number of measures which members from parties on this side of the House have been suggesting and urging these many years, he would not have to suffer the slings and arrows of opposition motions and questions.
The three items which we think should be added to the motion are as follows. We think the government should be persuaded or should agree to give up profit and user-pay priority over service to shippers and the travelling public in Atlantic Canada-for that matter, in all of Canada. Because of our climate and geography it is inevitable that all Canadians must equitably share the costs of transportation. That is particularly important for development in the Atlantic region, as well as in the west and the north. Confederation was not built on user-pay, and our climate and geography has not changed since then.
User-pay goes back to the MacPherson royal commission of 1961, which treated the concept of transport for development purposes as outdated. Some 20 years later every day in all regions of Canada we see how outdated the recommendation of the MacPherson report is. If we were to follow that policy through to its logical conclusion, it might also be possible to shrink Canada from 4,000 miles to 400 miles. It might also be possible to level the Rocky Mountains. That policy of user-pay and profitability taking priority over the provision of adequate transportation services to all regions of this country is doomed to fail. If it does succeed it is doomed to do irrevocable harm to our unity, more so than even the present debate on the Constitution.
I do not believe that it was appropriate for the previous Conservative government to send a directive calling for increases in port fees because that was simply carrying on at all costs the policy of user-pay profit which had been introduced by the previous Liberal government under a former minister of transport whom the voters finally caught up with.
The government should develop an industrial strategy providing Atlantic Canadian employment in building a modern and updated transportation system. There should be public investment to upgrade railways right across Canada. Rail steel is produced at Sydney, Nova Scotia and freight cars are produced at Trenton, Nova Scotia. I am happy to say that Saskatchewan, other provinces and the federal government bought many of the hopper cars from Trenton. But what about reefer cars for the movement of potatoes? The Newfoundland railway should be converted to standard gauge and curves should be straightened. This alone would consume enough steel to keep production at Sydney going for at least six months.
We need 21 vessels for CN Marine coastal and ferry services. We need a policy to create a merchant marine, support the Canadian shipbuilding industry and use short take-off and landing aircraft to serve coastal and northern communities. We do not need an elitist STOL service to handle business executives, MPs and deputy ministers between Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa; they can take the train.
We need public investment in urban transit in all cities in Atlantic Canada. We need multimodal stations to reduce terminal costs so that buses, railways and airlines can combine their operations, thus reducing costs to the travelling public. We need a more modernized VIA Rail service. This requires a higher priority from the national government.
Before I run out of time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to move an amendment to the main motion and continue my remarks for as long as you and the members of the House are prepared to allow me. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Powell River:
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a semi-colon, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"10. putting profits and user-pay ahead of service to Atlantic Canada;
11.	failing to develop an industrial strategy to create employment in Atlantic
Canada by building a modern transportation system; and
12.	failing to modernize rail passenger service in Atlantic Canada."
I believe that my amendment is relevant to, and a suitable addition to, the main motion proposed by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East. I hope it is acceptable not only to him and his colleagues, but also to the minister.
In the building of an industrial strategy or in the building of a strong economy, to use the words of some government cabinet ministers, transportation is an essential foundation to the success of an industrial strategy, a growing economy and full employment. Unless we can move goods and people fairly as well as efficiently, then any economic plans, private, public or governmental, cannot succeed. We should also have a policy in place which quits discriminating against people and their goods in this country because of where they happen to live or are located.
March 17, 1981

The Minister of Transport could set an example and lead the way in co-operating with the provinces and the territories for a system of equalized and/or subsidized transportation costs, freight rates and fares. When it costs $2 or $3 for a quart of milk in the Arctic but only 75 cents or $1 down south, surely that is discrimination. It is strange how provinces can equalize the price of liquor-I have been known to take the odd drink. Provinces can equalize the price of liquor from one end of the province to the other but they cannot do it with milk, fresh fruit and vegetables, propane and heating oils, flour and sugar, all of which are essential goods. This could be done for people on the Atlantic coast, the Pacific coast and those in northern Canada. As long as this government, or any government, adheres to the principles and theories of the 1890s when it considers transportation matters, we will fail to do the kind of job we could be doing.
Atlantic Canada needs a rebuilding of its transportation system. It needs electrified rail lines, additional rolling stock, and improved ferry services provided at cost or less than cost. I would prefer the latter, because at cost fares would have to increase. That cost should be borne by the nation as a whole, whether the cost is incurred on the Atlantic coast or the Pacific coast.
These kinds of transportation services will provide the type of infrastructure and foundation which will allow Atlantic industry to sell and ship to central Canada, to the United States, or overseas, since there are not enough people in Atlantic Canada to provide a market for all its potential production capacities. These people have to move their goods out of Atlantic Canada. We have seen too many instances where home industries in Atlantic Canada went bankrupt because they could not compete due to transportation costs and inadequacies, or compete with goods coming into central Canada from other parts of the world or the United States.
I hope the House will support our amendment and the motion of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Today, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative opposition is moving a motion condemning the policy of the government and particularly the conduct of the Minister of Transport on nine issues
Transportation
which, of course, have to do with transportation, particularly as it affects the Atlantic provinces. And just now the spokesman for the New Democratic Party has raised three more issues. I am pleased with the somewhat academic tone of the debate so far because I too am interested in giving hon. members as much information as possible so that the public at large will be in a better position to see what is going on.
Since we now have twelve topics, I will not be able to cover them all. For my part, I will speak to paragraph 1 concerning the use of transportation as a tool of national and regional development which, it is said here has been abandoned. Then I will go on to paragraph 6 of the motion which states that there has been a serious deterioration in freight rate structures, and paragraph 7 concerning the legislation which deals with ports, the Maritime Code and coastal shipping and which, according to the hon. member who moved this motion, has not been introduced in the House. And, as in his case, my colleagues will deal with the other topics. My colleagues from Moncton (Mr. McCauley), Egmont (Mr. Henderson), Restigouche (Mr. Harquail), Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons), Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) and Northumberland-Mirami-chi (Mr. Dionne) will deal with the other topics, namely the CN Express offices, CN Marine and its ferries, the Charlottetown airport, the St. John's syncro-lift facility, certain types of railroad cars, and potatoes of course. They will address themselves to all those subjects and this evening, probably around 9.30 p.m., the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael), whom I am pleased to have as parliamentary secretary, will gather all questions left unanswered and clean up the whole slate. This way, Mr. Speaker, we hope to answer the numerous questions raised in this motion. Before going any further- [English]
-I would like to say that the department and the minister have not neglected consulting with the governments and people of the Atlantic provinces. This subject was mentioned by the mover of the motion. I want to assure the House that the mechanism of consultation between governments has been reactivated. It has been pretty slow in recent times. In the last years, particularly in Newfoundland, a federal-provincial committee of Atlantic region transportation officials has been meeting quite regularly. As a matter of fact, it is meeting today in Ottawa.
I may add that I have had discussions with all my provincial counterparts in their own capitals, and in Ottawa and Toronto in the last year. I am going to St. John's, Newfoundland, at the end of this month for purposes of negotiation. There will probably be announcements of major importance, particularly with respect to the Newfoundland railway.
On the first point, the national transportation policy, there is action. The motion says that the minister has been abandoning the use of transportation as a tool of national and regional economic development. I am quite surprised by this perception because my impression is that we have been adding to it. In my view, the federal government, through Transport Canada par-

March 17, 1981
Transportation
ticularly, is very much present in the transportation systems of the provinces; all $564 million worth of presence, if one counts in dollars, and a much higher per capita presence-$252- than anywhere else in Canada. That presence is recognized in all modes of transportation: railways, ferries, coastal services, search and rescue, urban transportation, airports, highways, etc.
The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forre-stall) regrets that the National Transportation Act does not make specific reference to the objective of regional development. He knows better than I do that previous attempts at legislating this particular preoccupation have failed. There is no time to bring in a bill on that subject now. It would be damaging and sad if the government-this one and previous ones-did not give quite a lot of attention to the use of transportation as an instrument of regional development.
What about the impact of improvement ports on regional development? Consider what took place in Halifax, for example, concerning the building of the Fairview Cove at the second terminal. There is the proposal to build a potash facility at Saint John. There is also the matter of improved air facilities and services within as well as to and from the region.
At the time, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East approved the government's decision to allow EPA instead of CP Air to fly direct from Halifax to Toronto as a way of strengthening the economic base of EPA. He must be even more pleased now because Halifax is also being served by CP Air from Montreal and other points, with the exception of Toronto. Yesterday I heard that Air Canada had announced a non-stop Calgary-Halifax route for the coming months. I am sure his colleagues from Newfoundland rejoice in the new airport facilities on the Labrador coast. There are four of them and more to come. A new service facility is being built at Gander. I could go on and illustrate the impact of ferry subsidies and the improved services.
A moment ago the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) told us that the government should ignore profits when setting its transportation policies in Canada as a whole, and in the Atlantic provinces in particular. Most of us know that the rate of subsidization of ferries in the Atlantic area is considerable. In the last ten years, cost recovery has been reduced from 23 per cent to 20 per cent. If that is not the abandonment of profit for the purpose of regional development, I wonder what is. The same applies to the impact of the freight subsidy and the impact of federally-supported highway construction on cutting down distances and linking various centres in the Atlantic provinces.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I fail to see that the use of transportation and transportation policies to support economic, national and regional development has been weakened in any way. As a matter of fact, I think it has been strengthened and this will be demonstrated in the coming months.
Paragraph 6 of the motion states that freight rate structures have experienced serious deterioration and claims that there
has been a "loss of the traditional parity between river and coastal ports". I have notes enough here for the next three hours, Mr. Speaker, but that would be a Castro-type speech!
The first point I want to deal with under this heading concerns rail freight rates. There are numerous studies available dealing with freight rates in the Atlantic provinces. They conclude that freight rates in the Atlantic region are higher than the national average. This is a fact and it can be explained by what is referred to as the "commodity mix". That is, the mix of density of traffic, length of hauls, nature of the goods being transported and so on. It would take too much time to explain how that works and it is not peculiar to the Atlantic provinces; it is a national and international phenomenon. The same situation is experienced all over the world.
The difference between Atlantic rates and national rates reflects the relatively low rates in western Canada for such long haul commodities as coal and grain and the relatively short haul rates for Atlantic region commodities.
In the Atlantic provinces 80 per cent of rail traffic is in manufactured goods which originate or terminate there. The traffic is mostly short haul and, for obvious reasons, short haul is more expensive than long haul. However, Atlantic region freight rates compare favourably with those in Quebec and Ontario where most of its competition is. If hon. members would care for more information on this subject, I would be glad to send them notes that I have used today. I do not see how we can speak of "serious deterioration" when this phenomenon has been constant in the history of Canadian transportation.
As was indicated in question period today, the difference in freight rates has been identified by Premier Buchanan in recent days as one of the reasons for the Dart Containerline company moving from Halifax to Montreal. As I said in question period, there will be many opportunities in the coming months for that point to be proved. Until now, I have not seen much evidence of it. As a matter of fact, the president of Dart and the president of Halterm, the operator of Terminal I at Halifax which is partly owned by the government of Nova Scotia, has said very clearly that freight rates, or the position of CN in CAST, has not been a factor in that decision. He called it a straight "business decision", justified by the particular circumstances of a number of shipping companies. In the opinion of the experts with whom I have talked, the rail rates in Halifax are fair and equitable now. Of course, there could be any number of debates about what is fair and equitable. I have asked my experts-compared to what? They gave me a stock of comparisons.
Rail freight rates between Halifax and central Canada, particularly Montreal, have gone up 177 per cent in the last ten years. Compare that to the freight rate increase between Montreal and Toronto of 220 per cent; compare it to the consumer price index which is 216 per cent; compare it to the shipping rates across the Atlantic which are 425 per cent. That is about all one can produce in terms of estimating what is fair.
My friends on the other side should also be aware, as I am sure they are, that CN has equalized its rates with the port of
March 17, 1981

Saint John in New Brunswick, which gives the port of Halifax 200 miles of free transportation.
So much for freight rates, Mr. Speaker. The other point that 1 wish to develop is what my friend the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East called "a loss of the traditional parity between river and coastal ports". 1 have investigated that matter with the help of my specialists. As far as I can see there are three factors that could change that "parity between river and coastal ports".
The first one could be the higher charges levied by the National Harbours Board. I have asked the National Harbours Board to do some research and give me the figures. 1 find, as a result, that harbour dues are charged on the gross registered tonnage of the vessel are the same for all east coast ports-Halifax, Saint John and Quebec. So there is no discrimination in the matter of harbour dues. Berthage dues, money paid on the movement of ships at the dock, is the same throughout all eastern Canadian ports, so there is no discrimination there either. These are the facts and if hon. members want to challenge them, they should bring forward some evidence.
Then there is the wharfage charge on the cargo. This is on the basis of $1.78 per metric ton for containers, throughout east coast ports. However, Halterm, operating out of Terminal No. I in Halifax, enjoys a 50 per cent rebate on all wharfage charges. No other port in Canada enjoys this special arrangement. It represents a degree of subsidization on the part of the National Harbours Board which in 1980 was estimated at $1.8 million. If one wants to talk about discrimination being exercised against Halifax, one must bring up contrary facts to those I am now placing before hon. members.
The next point is with reference to rental and the National Harbours Board. This was alluded to in today's question period. The fact is that for the first ten years Halterm was given a development contract of 15 cents per square foot. I repeat, this was for a period of ten years. After the ten years, an assessment was made of the fair market value and it indicated that an increase was called for, I think last December, from $388,000 to $1.76 million, a pretty big jump. This was referred to in question period today.
The National Harbours Board has known all about this. This increase was fairly assessed by two experts and the lower of the two assessments was chosen. Other contracts signed with lessees at the port of Halifax in recent months have been at the same level. Elalterm is entitled to appeal, and it is doing that through the Federal Court.
On the general subject of the situation in the port of Halifax, there are a number of people with more optimistic views than those expressed regarding the Dart move. Again, the move will not take place before the end of the year, as was mentioned by the Dart people. Yesterday Gary Blaikie, the executive director of the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Commission, made a speech in Halifax. He looked at the good side of things when analysing the development of containerization in the world today. He said that developments are taking place in the Caribbean, India, East Africa and so on. He saw Halifax,
Transportation
being in proximity to New York, as one of the prime locations for Canadian traffic. In a more positive and concrete way, he referred to a number of things that have taken place recently. For example, there is the contract that Ceres, which operates Terminal II at Fairview Cove, has with a Polish line and Soviet line representing 17,500 containers per year.
There is another piece of interesting news; I do not know whether my friends from the Atlantic have seen it. A news item of today states that 100,000 tons of flour will be shipped to the Soviet Union this year from Canada, most of which will be moved through Halifax, beginning next month. Are members opposite aware of that? The flour order is expected to provide steady work in Halifax for 300 longshoremen during the next four months.
I come back to my theme. If there is, as the mover of the motion says, a loss of traditional parity between river and coastal ports, my advice is that this is not caused by the National Harbours Board.
Another factor of disparity could be the Atlantic shipping rates which are determined by shipping conferences. As members know, these conferences are exempted from the rules of competition under the Shipping Conference Exemption Act of 1979. This is for the sake of stability and regularity of service.
I understand that shipping conferences can equalize the cost of shipping from point x in Europe to Halifax or Montreal. This is often a subject of debate in Canada. The exemption is valid from 1979 on for five years. Two years ago the CTC inquired into this subject. I tabled the CTC report on the operation of the shipping conferences yesterday. One can read in it that there has been no complaint about the operation of these conferences in Canada. Nevertheless, this is a subject of debate with arguments both for and against.
Another factor which might influence the traditional parity between river and coastal ports is the cost recovery by Transport Canada of navigational services. This was raised in the debate recently when some people said that the expenditure of the department on icebreaking in the St. Lawrence was "unfair competition" against the interests of the port of Halifax.
The subject is difficult because icebreaking is done for purposes other than navigation, such as the control of floods. There are other navigational aids to commercial transportation than icebreaking, so why choose this one and not others? There are also other ports in the Atlantic provinces which experience icing and come under the icebreaking program of the department. Be that as it may, it is estimated that the cost of icebreaking on the St. Lawrence and in the gulf is about $17 million. When that is divided by the commercial tonnage on the St. Lawrence and in the gulf, icebreaking aid can be assessed at the maximum, at $1.60 per ton, on the total cost of transportation. Experts say it is immaterial. So much for my analysis of freight rates, shipping rates and St. Lawrence rates.

speechtext:
In the next five mintues I will try to answer some of the questions raised by the hon. member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East. He asked about our coastal trade policy. He knows better than I that earlier legislation on the subject was opposed by the Atlantic provinces and others. A team from Transport Canada has had extensive consultations on the subject. I know the hon. member speaks regularly with the officials of Transport Canada to keep in touch with developments in the world of transportation. He may realize that coastal trade is not the issue he thought it might be when he first became interested in it. I understand that 95 per cent of the coastal trade in Canada is done in Canadian bottoms. That eliminates the subject as a dramatic issue.
On the second subject, that of a deep sea fleet, the hon. member knows of the deep, deep division on this among Canadian public opinion. I have been exposed to this reality at a number of meetings, for example with the forest industry of British Columbia. Reconciliation efforts are being made. I have had meetings with people on both sides of the issue. My predecessor did not exactly move the world on this issue either. He knows that shippers are afraid that sooner or later the government might force them to use Canadian registered ships. He knows also that Canadian shippers are afraid of what happened on the union side.
On the Maritime Code question the situation is that because of the degree of urgency, amendments to the Canada Shipping Act were passed by cabinet last December and we hope they will come to the House for implementation next fall. These amendments will be to complete the revision of part XX of that act regarding liability and compensation for pollution.
With respect to the totality, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) would say of the Maritime Code, my officials expect that cabinet will receive it by August, 1981, which indicates that it might come to the House for legislative action in the fall of 1982. So progress is being made.
We may be closer to success with regard to port policy. During the summer, and more recently, I regularly met with groups and members of port authorities. The marine administrator of my department has done a tremendous amount of work in recent months on this subject, and there is a paper coming to cabinet in the coming days. The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East is aware of the gist of the legislation that might develop from that paper. The general idea would be the creation of a national ports corporation, a maxi-corporation, as I call it, with much broader regional representation, and a number of mini-corporations in the different ports- Halifax, Montreal and Vancouver-with a much higher degree of management autonomy given to the local adminitra-tors. This is going to be very practical, down to earth and realistic, as the Minister of Transport is, and consequently I think it will have a good chance of being approved by Parliament.
Finally, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East said there was not enough philosophy, objectives, planning or sense
of orientation in matters of transport at this time in Canada. I would just like to put my two bits in. It is not a magnificent idea but one borrowed from others, like all ideas-no one has ever invented one-and I am trying to push it as hard as I can now because I think it makes sense.
Often enough today, I and others have referred to amounts of money the federal government is spending on transportation in the Atlantic provinces. Speaking very frankly, I am not at all sure that this money is always spent in the most worthwhile fashion. One of the reasons for this is the lack of planning and co-ordination between the interested parties. Another reason is the fear the provinces have of not getting all the help they can from the central government in each mode separately. I have been impressed by that. They tend to look at railways, ferries, air transportation and highways separately because in each case they feel they are in a better position in bargaining with the federal government.
To obviate that, and borrowing a chapter or two from the Sullivan report, we have offered to the Atlantic provinces in recent months a new approach which can be described in three words-multimodal, envelope and trade-off. Multimodal simply means that rail, highway, air transport and ferries will be looked upon together instead of in isolation. The envelope concept simply means that the money not spent in one province will not be returned to the Receiver General; it will be put in an envelope. The third word is trade-off. In that envelope it can be shifted from one mode to the other.
Now, I repeat, it is an idea that is not new at all but it makes sense, and personally I found it very well developed in the Sullivan report. So if the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East was looking for a philosophy, for a direction, there is one that he could accept. This is the sort of deal we expect to strike with Newfoundland in the coming days.
As for the railways, maybe yes, maybe no; we would like to include them in that approach. It is quite possible that the provinces will want to treat them separately; but on other matters that I am not at liberty to reveal today, this approach will be taken. Premier Peckford and Mr. Brett, who is the Newfoundland minister of transport, have given approval in their own assembly recently. We hope to carry the same approach to other Atlantic provinces. That is about all I wanted to say.

being discussed in this chamber today is that my party has some priorities that come ahead of the Constitution. speechtext:
Vote on it? We are not going to accept this load of garbage you are handing us; we will vote on it when we are ready and after it has been amply discussed. The government could postpone this debate and bring before this House the things they should be bringing forward on the economy, inflation, transportation and the like.
The minister just tolled the death knell for the hopes of Newfoundland for economic development, and that just fits in with the first clause of our non-confidence motion. We are censuring the government for abandoning the principle of the use of transportation as a tool of national and regional economic development. That is just what he said. He has come up with a new magic formula. It has to be one that is multimodal when he deals with the provinces. There is a certain envelope of spending and you will not get any more than that.
Then there are trade-offs. Well, how can there be trade-offs in the economic development of a region or province? How can you trade off a railway against decent road transportation? How can you trade off decent rail transportation against decent shipping transportation? Why should a region be expected to do that?
Central Canada has had all of these transportation modes for the last 114 years, but other areas of the country, like the Altantic provinces, have not. Why should we now be told to trade off? That is one of the three great points of this minister's policy. He is going to Newfoundland and saying: "Under the terms of union of 1949 we had to subsidize your ferry service across the gulf. We are going to take the amount of money that is costing us today and put it in your envelope, so there is $50 million or $60 million that you cannot have for other transportation needs in Newfoundland as a result of this alleged trade-off." That is not a trade-off; it was a constitutional right given to Newfoundland in 1949 and should not be in the envelope at all.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION PROBLEMS
speechtext:
So it is the death knell. This minister has been in office now for 13 months. He has been short-taken now for 13 months. What has he done? He has been looking, hesitating, obfuscating, bewailing, excusing and hand-wringing. He
Transportation
has been sighing. He has been crying. He is not doing, and he has been double-crossing.
What did he do? Where was his double-crossing? If the minister wants to know where he did the double-crossing, he did his double-crossing in Newfoundland when he changed the water transportation assistance directorate that his government promised it would move down to Newfoundland. He announced last year that the water transportation assistance directorate was no longer going to be transferred to Newfoundland, that he was reversing that policy because now there are more important policies. It was not going through. That was a commitment made in two elections, a solemn promise made to some of the employees transferred to Newfoundland, and the minister reversed that decision. He has been busy double-crossing, but he has not been acting.
Where are his transportation improvements? There have been very precious few that I can see. He did make one good decision, and that was on the route for EPA from Halifax to Toronto. I have to give the minister credit for that. He did the right thing there.
However, in area after area this government has no transportation policy. Its only policy is to squeeze the provinces, squeeze the regions, squeeze them till their pips squeak, give them the old talk about multimodal, give them the old talk about the famous envelope, give them the old talk about trade-offs till there is nothing left and no way for them to build up their economic development. 1 suggest that what we need here are six ministers to replace the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). We could have a minister of state for water transport, a minister of state for air transport, a minister of state for ground transport, a minister of state for Atlantic transport, a minister of state for western transport and a minister of state for excuses. All six of those together might be able to do a job which this minister certainly is not doing today. We need a minister whose whole time is devoted to excuses.
In my own province of Newfoundland the Trans-Canada Highway agreement terminates on March 31, 1981. This is March 17, St. Patrick's Day, and in 14 days' time this agreement expires. The minister has not concluded a new agreement with the government of Newfoundland. He has not told them what money is available. They are looking for $75 million in another three-year agreement. Just two weeks before this agreement expires there is no decision reached. We have the most miserable, spavined Trans-Canada highway in the whole country. It is a narrow, double-laned highway badly needing upgrading and repairing. It is the main route through Newfoundland and there are no trade-offs. That highway has to be strengthened and improved, or transportation comes to a halt in Newfoundland, but the minister has not yet entered into an agreement. It should be a 90 per cent federal and 10 per cent provincial agreement, not 50-50. That is one priority the minister should have, and he has apparently been doing nothing about it.

March 17, 1981
Transportation
There has been only one DREE agreement signed since the present government took office and we had the forestry agreement in January. They are still waiting to sign a coastal Labrador agreement. Although the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) represents Labrador, he is doing nothing to expedite that agreement. He should be ashamed of himself. That is the only proposed DREE agreement which has any funding in it for roads. The Straits road in coastal Labrador badly needs repair, but the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will no longer spend any funds on roads in Newfoundland. The Witless Bay line in my own district is very important for economic development in the region and for transportation of products from fish plants. The road from Trepassey to Peter's River in my own district of St. John's West badly needs reconstruction and paving to enable fishery products to be taken out and transported in, workers to get to their jobs and the like. Nothing has been done. The government will not have anything to do with roads under DREE agreements.
Then there is the Newfoundland government's study on the Newfoundland railway; the minister has announced no decisions on that. The minister is going to Newfoundland at the end of the month to announce a new containerization plan for the Newfoundland railway. They are going to attempt to go to containerization to help save that railway or to see if it can become economic. But I am concerned, as are the people of Newfoundland, about the 300 jobs that are now redundant and the additional jobs that may become redundant under that agreement. So I hope when the minister goes to Newfoundland he will deal adequately with that problem and see that these people get generous treatment, retraining, other jobs, early generous pensions or whatever is necessary.
With regard to the Deer Lake and Stephenville airports, I hope the minister-the member for that district has said this, and 1 hope he is correct-is going to keep both those airports operating as well as the airport in St. Anthony. I hope the minister is also going to start spending some money on the airport at St. John's. We have a major airport at St. John's which this government has always been prejudiced against. That airport handled 580,000 passengers in 1980, but a 100 per cent increase in air traffic volume in St. John's is expected in the next ten years due to the oil and gas development off the coast of Newfoundland. A 100 per cent increase in the next ten years, yet this government does nothing. It is not even improving the instrument landing system, as it is at other Canadian airports. I quote a release dated March 9:
Present planning calls for replacement of ILS at the following airports: Windsor, Whitehorse, Frobisher, Terrace, Moncton, Dorval, Sault Ste. Marie, Churchill, Thompson, Sudbury, Toronto, Halifax, Yellowknife, Stephenville, Hamilton, Fort St. John, Abbotsford, Edmonton, Sandspit and Lethbridge.
Sandspit comes ahead of St. John's airport which handled 580,000 passengers last year, with a 100 per cent increase in the next five to ten years anticipated. Yet this government will not even instal, a first-class ILS at St. John's airport. These are the kinds of things the minister should be giving his attention to. Never mind the multi-modal excuses. Never mind the envelope. Never mind the trade-offs. There can be no
trade-offs for proper transportation services in the more remote areas of Canada.
What about the patronage aspect? Patronage is overloading the whole transportation system. This minister is up to his ankles, up to his knees, he is approaching his chest in patronage. Here is one examples. The minister was written to on February 19 by the Newfoundland Shipowners, Agents and Brokers Association of St. John's-they represent Newfoundland shipowners-about a complaint concerning Canadian National and their tender operations in connection with services to Labrador. Their complaint to the minister went in almost a month ago. There has been no reply yet. Their complaint was that on January 7, 1980, CN Marine advertised a tender call for an ISU container-carrying vessel. The specifications for that vessel referred particularly in specification 5, to the vessel having derricks or cranes capable of handling safe-working loads of 22.5 tons specification, implying that the vessel had to be used in small ports. I have the specifications here. "Vessels should preferably be equipped with bow thrusters for requirement of operating in smaller coastal ports". Derricks or cranes were required.
The people who belong to the Newfoundland Shipowners, Agents and Brokers Association tendered for this vessel on the basis of these specifications. They located a suitable vessel that would meet those specifications. Tenders closed, and after tenders closed, lo and behold, the final announcement is made by CN on February 10 that they have awarded a contract for this vessel to Coastal Shipping Limited, but not for the kind of boat that they specified in their tender call. It is for a new roll-on, roll-off container shipping service between St. John's and Goose Bay, Labrador, only. The vessel does not have to go into small coastal ports. The vessel does not have to have derricks or cranes capable of handling 22!6-ton loads.
CN called a tender for one kind of vessel, publicized it and only allowed 23 days to put a bid in. The people who were not on the inside, knowing nothing about the fact that they wanted some other kind of vessel, located the kind of vessel that was specified, and then they were told that their vessel was not suitable, that the lowest tender was submitted by Coastal Shipping Limited, who tendered for a roll-on, roll-off vessel. Who is Coastal Shipping Limited? Coastal Shipping Limited is Mr. Mel Woodward, the biggest Liberal in the Happy Valley-Goose Bay area, a man heart to heart, brain to brain and toe to toe, with the Minister of National Revenue. This cries out for an investigation. Why was this method used? On page 2 of their letter to the minister, they asked why the time permitted for tendering was limited to 23 days-
-in light of the fact that the service was not scheduled to commence for some four months;
Why did the specifications require a vessel equipped with derricks or cranes when presumably roll-on, roll-off was acceptable and indeed now appears to be preferable for the service intended;
Why was there a reference in Specification 8 to "smaller coastal ports" when the service is actually St. John's to Goose Bay?
They were going to make this same Mr. Melvin Woodward a director of Petro-Canada until they found out that he represented Imperial Oil Limited up in Goose Bay and all
March 17, 1981

along the coast of Labrador. What are they going to do with him now? They are going to make him a director of the Bank of Canada, I hear. He is going to replace Spencer Lake. So, Mr. Minister, let us have a quick investigation. It was only a month ago that it was brought to the minister's attention. This situation cries out for investigation into the reasons that CN adopted this peculiar procedure. The whole transportation area is rife with this kind of, let us call it suspicious circumstance that requires explanation, particularly when you find that the Coastal Shipping company have the preferred deal. They must have had inside information as they happen to be also connected with one of the most prominent Liberals in Newfoundland, a man who was a member of the House of Assembly for that district at one time.
So do not talk to us about multimodal, do not talk to us about envelopes and do not talk to us about trade-offs. We have seen the trade-offs; Mr. Woodward just got a trade-off. What he got for the trade-off I do not know, but we got a trade-off. As long as the minister is in that portfolio, he will learn.
With regard to the syncro-lift facility, one of the most dastardly deeds ever done by the Government of Canada was to stop construction of the synchrolift for the CN dockyard in St. John's West, in my district, last fall. At page 2340 of the estimates of the Department of Public Works for 1981-82 we find: "St. John's syncro-lift dry-docking facility, $11,500,000". All that work has been stopped. The Minister of National Revenue was asked why, and I am told that on the air the other day he said: "We could not go ahead in our first year in office and spend money in a district that was held by the opposition". Imagine, Mr. Speaker, he candidly admitted that this was the basis on which the decision was made!
Economic development and the creation of 200 jobs in Newfoundland at the dockyard-one of the most sensible propositions that was ever made-does not matter to this government. All that matters to this government is the most odious kind of patronage. It reeks of it. The government is up to its knees in it; it is up to its nose in patronage practice; it is over its nose in it so it cannot even smell it.
What has happened to syncro-lift now, Mr. Speaker? The Newfoundland government, the second poorest government in Canada at this time, is providing the money to Canadian National so that they will go ahead with syncro-lift. The province is putting up $10 million for the project; $6.5 million alone to be repaid from hoped for profits, and the rest from subsidy and interest costs. The province is forced to do that because the Government of Canada, which owns that dockyard and which has CN operate it for them, through political spite, through political meanness, through political chicanery, through political treachery and trickery of the worst type, cancelled a project which they had promised before the election of 1979 and again promised through their candidate in 1980 because it was in a district held by a Conservative. Well, that will be a district held by a Conservative for 100 years to

I think my time is running out, Mr. Speaker. We have multidimensional, multimodal, multitudinous problems.
