speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate condemning the failure of the government to deal adequately with national transportation matters, and specifically condemning the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin).
Transportation issues are a matter of vital importance to the whole of this vast country. I would like to spend the next few minutes emphasizing the importance of a strong, functional and efficient transportation system to my province of Prince Edward Island, a province which, like many others, has been sorely neglected by the federal Department of Transport.
Over 100 years ago, in 1873, Prince Edward Island entered confederation. One of the conditions upon which it joined this country was that the federal government should establish and maintain transportation links between Prince Edward Island and the mainland of Canada. I quote:
Federal authorities agreed to take over the railway guarantee and establish and maintain efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers . .. between the Island and the mainland of the dominion, winter and summer-
In 1873, as today, it is vital that Prince Edward Island have an efficient, functional transportation system. It is unfortunate that the federal government has seen fit to renege on its transportation commitments to Prince Edward Island. In all facets of Island transportation-rail service, shipping by water, air transportation, highway development and car ferry services-the federal government has failed to live up to its promises to provide and maintain efficient service for Islanders.
In order for our agricultural and fisheries industries to remain viable, an upgrading of the systems that transport their products to market must take place. The tourism industry also depends heavily on how efficiently the transportation service to and on Prince Edward Island is operating. We need better roads, better port facilities, an improved ferry and rail service and an overhaul of air service. We need the assistance of the federal Department of Transport, assistance which has been sadly lacking.
8342

March 17, 1981
Transportation
One of the Island's main transportation worries is the need for rail improvements. There is a definite need to upgrade and maintain rail lines, and a need for research and development on improving rail service. In recent years there has been a trend toward shipping by road rather than by rail. Islanders feel strongly that rail service will always be needed, and therefore it should be properly maintained and its efficiency increased.
In the present situation where eastern Canada is completely dependent upon its offshore petroleum supplies, it is only prudent to achieve fuel conservation by carrying more of our goods by rail and less by truck. Truck freighting also places a heavy burden on the provincial department of highways, because due to our soil conditions and unavailability of suitable road-building materials, coupled with our climate, it is almost impossible, without prohibitive expense, to try to maintain roads to carry a large volume of heavy trucks. Owing to the increased tractor-trailer truck traffic over Prince Edward Island highways, the roads are deteriorating rapidly, and this is in part due to the reduction in proper rail service.
The way Canadian National has neglected the rail system on Prince Edward Island is deplorable. Canadian National is even considering abandoning 80 miles of Prince Edward Island's total of 275 miles of rail line. Prince Edward Island needs its rail system and everything possible should be done to retain it. The federal government must consider, as a high priority, action to have Canadian National rebuild its railway lines in Prince Edward Island, and otherwise increase its efficiency to reverse the present trend toward road freighting.
The present condition of the Prince Edward Island railbed and level of service has made it difficult for Island shippers to meet their objectives. Prince Edward Island potato growers have to use obsolete rail cars and face inadequate or wrongly placed storage capacity, and misunderstandings over costs, which have produced an unsatisfactory transportation system. Given the nature of the highly competitive potato industry, which I am sure hon. members are aware is a major contributor to the Prince Edward Island economy, it is essential that Island shippers are able to meet stringent market demands in terms of quality of product and delivery time. Island shippers have been experiencing difficulty in obtaining sufficient equipment, both insulated boxcars and piggyback units. The potato industry is most optimistic this year, after three disastrous years, and early movements, particularly by rail, attest to this fact.
It is essential that Canadian National provide the Island, this year and in the future, with sufficient equipment to move the potato crop. The federal government cannot afford to neglect this important aspect of Prince Edward Island's transportation and economy.
I want to touch briefly on a matter which I have already mentioned in reference to rail service, and it is with regard to the highways on Prince Edward Island and in the other two maritime provinces. As a means of achieving greater uniformity in trucking regulations, Transport Canada and the Atlantic provinces undertook a cost-shared, primary highway upgrading in 1977. The first phase of this program was completed over a period of three years, and the maritime provinces- Newfoundland is negotiating separately-are seeking federal funding to proceed on the same cost-sharing basis with phase 2 of the program.
To further the federal objective of achieving greater uniformity of trucking regulations, it is necessary that the federal government and the Department of Transport continue costsharing the highway strengthening program begun in 1977 with the maritime provinces. The minister should take immediate steps to provide funding for the second phase of this vitally important program so that the maritime provinces can resume construction.
The quality of transportation within Prince Edward Island is an important factor in determining whether Islanders are willing and able to live in the rural areas of the province. The importance of the paving and maintenance of Island roads cannot be too strongly emphasized. Prince Edward Island depends on the cost-sharing arrangement with the federal government so that its roads can continue to be reconstructed and upgraded. I hope the federal government will choose not to disappoint us in this respect, as it has on other transportation issues.
I would like to dwell on an aspect of the marine transport system which affects Prince Edward Island greatly, and that is the ferry service linking the Island to the mainland of Canada. The ferry system provides a vital link to Prince Edward Island. Ferry travel should cost no more than travel over a similar distance on the Trans-Canada highway. The cost of travelling on the ferries should be the same as it would cost an ordinary person to travel nine miles by car on a section of the Trans-Canada highway. Therefore, it appalls me to think that right now Treasury Board is considering a Transport Canada recommendation to increase most maritime ferry fares by an average of 12.5 per cent. I am even more appalled by the fact that neither the provincial government of Prince Edward Island nor any interested Island organizations were given the opportunity to review the Canadian Transport Commission recommendations and decision concerning ferry rate increases.
Many Island industries and Islanders depend entirely for their livelihood on the marine transportation links to Prince Edward Island. Prince Edward Island's tourism industry, in particular, is directly affected by ferry rate increases; in excess of 50 per cent of the visitors to Prince Edward Island come from the Atlantic region. Any additional ferry rate increase at this time would make travel to Prince Edward Island an additional hardship within a region of Canada that now has more than its share of regional economic disparities.
The tourism industry is a major one in Prince Edward Island, and about half of the traffic that comes to the Island comes by ferry. Tourism has received inequitable treatment over the past years relative to ferry rates when compared with other segments of Prince Edward Island's economy, and any unilateral rate increases at this time would further compound the inequities. Tourism is a major industry on Prince Edward Island and is labour-intensive, which is the type of industry the
March 17, 1981

Island and Canada need because of the major unemployment problem throughout the country today. Increasing ferry rates would do a great injustice to the economy of Prince Edward Island as it would have an inflationary effect which would hurt all sectors of the Island economy.
I have in my hand a telex, dated today, which was sent to the Minister of Transport. It is from Don Reid, the president of the Tourism Industry Association of P.E.I. He starts out by saying:
Dear Mr. Minister:
Your telex of March 13, 1981, leaves little doubt that it is the intention of Transport Canada to proceed with ferry rate increases not having truly taken into consideration the strong objections of the members of this major industry in Prince Edward Island.
He goes on:
To say it is regrettable that rate changes could not be dealt with earlier is somewhat absurd, considering the fact that CN Marine had submitted rate proposals as early as July 1980, and no consultative action was taken with this major industry and, to the best of our knowledge little if any consultation was conducted with the provincial government or CN Marine-
To say that bus tours or the distribution of schedules would not be unduly affected is as good as calling the major bus carriers and CN Marine fly-by-nite operators who do not have to budget for their operations.
The telex is rather long. I will dispense with reading all of it, and go to the last paragraph:
We again urge you and your colleagues to forgo the application of any changes in ferry rates to P.E.I. and immediately commence serious discussions with the appropriate government departments, carriers and industries for the 1982 season and beyond.

speechtext:
If the federal government insists on going ahead with ferry rate increases, it could at least afford affected parties an opportunity to discuss, negotiate and present objective concerns. There must be consultation between the federal government, tourist operators and others affected by an increase in ferry rates. But then again, this government does not place a very high priority on consultation, does it? I hope the Minister of Transport will ensure that ferry rates do not increase until such time as a complete review has taken place, and all sectors of the Island economy are afforded ample opportunity to present their views on the matter.
Before I leave the question of ferries, I would like to comment on another aspect of the Prince Edward Island ferry system where the federal government is again dragging its heels. The report of Transport Canada's Prince Edward Island-mainland transportation study, released in 1976, recommended that a new 150-car vessel be placed in service between Wood Island, Prince Edward Island, and Caribou, Nova Scotia, by 1979. The proposed vessel would greatly reduce the intolerable congestion at the ferry terminals and thus would help eliminate one of the worst barriers to the continued development of the Island's basic industries. It would also substantially increase the efficiency of the Wood Island-Caribou ferry operation as the ratio of vehicle capacity to crew members would more than double. It is now 1981 and there is
Transportation
no new ferry. When will the minister heed the recommendation of his department and proceed with the construction of the required new ferry?
Prince Edward Island's other link to the mainland is through its air service. At this time we who live on the Island are waiting for the start of construction of a new terminal building for the Charlottetown airport, and we have been waiting for a very long time. The Charlottetown airport redevelopment has become a matter of considerable concern to Prince Edward Island. There have been conflicting reports and controversy regarding this project, as well as a lack of good communications.
Three years ago, the federal and provincial governments reached an agreement on the building of a new airport for Prince Edward Island. Construction of a new terminal and related projects was to begin in September, 1978, at a cost of $21.5 million. Shortly after this agreement was reached. Treasury Board ordered that the size of the proposed airport terminal be reduced, to save $1.5 million. The federal government then proceeded with plans to design a scaled-down airport terminal building, with a second and separate control tower. The airport was to be expandable as the need might arise.
The people of Prince Edward Island have waited long enough for their badly-needed new airport terminal building. The prolonged delay in the construction of the new terminal building since the federal-provincial agreement was reached, not to mention the additional cost of the redesign ordered by the Treasury Board, has actually increased the cost of the project rather than reduced it. In the past, the Liberal government wasted hundreds of thousands of dollars on a constant patching up and extension of the present terminal facilities. This is another indication of the inefficiency of the Department of Transport. In the meantime, the deplorable congestion at the old terminal has worsened to the point that the airport can no longer meet current needs, much less keep up with the increase in passenger usage and cargo handling which is projected for the future.
As the gateway to Prince Edward Island for many visitors, the existing wartime-vintage airport is nothing less than a disgrace to our province. I sincerely mean that. Municipal airports in many small communities across Canada provide better facilities than our own on Prince Edward Island. Yet our airport is required to serve an entire province, not just one municipality. The continued postponement and delay in proceeding with the terminal building component of the Charlottetown airport redevelopment project has inconvenienced the travelling public; it has prolonged the uncertainty with respect to transportation planning in Prince Edward Island; it has added greatly to the frustration of Islanders with respect to federal projects; and it has increased the cost to the taxpayer beyond what would have been the original cost had the project been pursued with dispatch.
There is also concern about the fact that Charlottetown is the only provincial capital that does not have provision for customs clearance at its airport, and there are no plans for

March 17, 1981
Transportation
such provision in the proposed new airport terminal building. This means that flights from outside the country, including charters from the United States, cannot land at Charlottetown. Prince Edward Island is losing potential tourists and tourist dollars because of this fact. Because there is no customs clearance in Charlottetown airport, Islanders who want to go out of the country cannot go directly from Charlottetown but have to go to Halifax, Montreal or Toronto for customs clearance.
We in Prince Edward Island should not have to settle for such second-class treatment at the hands of the federal government. Transport Canada should proceed without further delay with the construction of a new air terminal building. The Department of Transport should proceed in accordance with the design that was completed and agreed to in 1977. We on the Island need a well-equipped air terminal which will meet our needs for the foreseeable future and which will be a credit to our province, not a disgrace.
At noon today we met with Mr. Bill Rowe of Air Canada. He advised us that Air Canada will spend $68,000 on the terminal at Charlottetown as it is in such deplorable condition.
There is another issue with which I should like to deal briefly in the time remaining to me, Mr. Speaker. It concerns the reduction in the number of CN Express offices in Charlottetown. On January 30 I put a question to the Minister of Transport which is reported at page 6735 of Hansard as follows:
My question to the minister is: will he now tell this House if the Express offices in Charlottetown and some other maritime centres will remain open and what level of service can be expected?
My supplementary question was as follows:
-I would like to ask the minister how many of the 41 employees in Charlottetown will be allowed to retain their jobs.
The minister responded by saying that the figures would be repeated on Monday. On Monday nothing happened. Five days later, on February 4, my colleague the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan) asked the following question of the same minister:
Will the minister tell the House how many CN Express employees will be kept in the two centres? Could he also tell the House what level of service will be maintained in those two Express terminals-
The minister's answer, in part, was as follows:
The employment level will be at about half what it is now, that is 19 people in Charlottetown-
I have before me, Mr. Speaker, the contents of a letter which were related to me by telephone. On March 16, Mr. R. O. Waterton, the regional manager of CN Express in Moncton, sent a letter to Mr. MacPherson, the manager of CN Express in Charlottetown. A copy of the letter was sent to Mr. J. L. Diorio, general manager of operations for CN Express in Montreal. Mr. Waterton's interpretation of the agreement at CN Express Charlottetown is that it provides for about 19 jobs, consisting of the 14 established positions, including the manager, with five spare and relief. The five spare and relief are to cover all operations under the union agreement, including the Servo-Centre, the Enter-Model, which is piggyback,
and the maintenance shop. It would therefore appear that there are not 19 positions, since 14 is not 19. The minister has not fulfilled his commitment made in this House on February 4, 1981, as recorded at page 6874 of Hansard, when he said that there would be 19 positions in Charlottetown.
I conclude by saying that the people in P.E.I. and the people at CN Express are terribly disappointed that the minister has not fulfilled his promise.

Mr. Speaker, I want to express my congratulations to you on being elevated to the Chair. By way of explanation, this is my first opportunity to do so. As a colleague from the province of New Brunswick, 1 am delighted in the choice and I wish you well.

I want to extend my congratulations to you and to wish you well in the discharge of your duties.

I wish to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) who I am sure laboured long hours to prepare this list of nine detailed and complex items relating to transportation, specifically in Atlantic Canada. It affords me an opportunity to speak at length with regard to all aspects of transportation, not only in the Atlantic region, and to refer specifically to problems in the northern part of New Brunswick.
Before dealing with some of those problems, I want to respond to some of the remarks by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass). While we have only had the opportunity of observing that member in recent times, I found it strange that he was not thankful for the funds directed to his province by the federal government which, on close examination, are substantial. That province with a population of 120,000 enjoys approximately 80 cents on the dollar of federal money transferred to it for all its operations, not to mention the dollars spent by Transport Canada and CN Marine which provide First class ferry service, comparable to that anywhere in Canada and in many other countries.
On many occasions I have used that service to take my family for our annual vacation to beautiful Prince Edward Island. I have personally utilized the ferry service from Tor-mentine to Borden. The equipment and the service provided cannot be criticized. I realize the hon. member for Malpeque is from that province and was expressing his concerns, but I should point out the seriousness on the part of this administration in putting a substantial number of federal dollars into the CN ferry service between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
Another point that could be flagged is the fact that the hon. member for Malpeque did not enlighten us as to why all these things were not done when his party was in government. There was equal opportunity at that time for the then minister of transport and his cabinet colleagues to do what he complained
March 17, 1981

of this afternoon. I did not think it wise to allow those comments to go by without referring to the fact that the present administration has consistently placed high priority on the matter of transportation.
Where would Atlantic Canada be without Transport Canada? I am sure the hon. member who introduced this motion on behalf of the official opposition has thought over this question for many years. He is one of the benefactors of the many millions of dollars transferred to the Atlantic region in one form or another, whether in the general transfer payments, contained in the main estimates in transport or in some other way.
1 agree we cannot expect to have progress without a positive policy to develop all aspects of transportation in Atlantic Canada. We certainly have not reached the time when we can move away from that position and turn our backs on transportation. The Atlantic region is still in the very important developing stage.
In relation to the first item in the motion regarding regional development, I wholeheartedly endorse the need to continuously allocate funds within the budget to developing transportation, surface, water and air. We are no different from any other part of Canada; we are no different than any other region when it comes to those needs.
In the province of New Brunswick we have had a sad experience with the present provincial administration regarding the fairness of planning, the strategy of developing priorities and allocating funds to this very important matter. That administration cannot expect the handout of federal funds forever. If they have not already received the message, let me make it clear this afternoon. If they do not mature in their thinking and realize that this cannot be permitted to continue in the fashion it has over the years, they might well find themselves in the position of having to find other ways and means to prop up and finance some of their pet projects in that province.
If the Premier of New Brunswick and the transportation minister there do not soon get their act together, they will not only be behind the eight ball, but they will be so far out of touch with reality in this country in terms of transportation it will not be funny. They are our gateways and they need the concern of the Minister of Transport. They should be given an equal break.
One other item to which I should like to refer is that mentioned by the hon. member for Restigouche when he
referred to the slow progress in the construction of route No.

I ask him to make another speech at a later date, after he has read the initial agreement for the construction of route No. 11 undertaken jointly by the Government of Canada and the government of New Brunswick, and after he has read the revised agreement and the reduction in the cost shared by the federal government, so that he will understand, in part at least, why that road has not progressed at the speed he would desire. The reason is the sharp reduction in the cost-sharing responsibility of the Government of Canada.
The number of ways in which transportation serves Atlantic Canada is so great it is impossible to mention them all. I want to mention the town of McAdam. The town of McAdam had a veneer mill established with DREE money. That mill found it could not ship its product by rail to destinations in Canada for two reasons: uncertainty of delivery-and I would like the minister to hear this-and the excessive damage caused in transit. Neither the manufacturer nor the receiver could accept the damage. Why was that damage occurring? It was occurring because regulations have been ignored by the Department of Transport, shunting practices have changed on the railroad at the various new humpyards which are there, and the speed with which cars connect is excessive; so damage occurs. Therefore they were forced, whether they wished or not, to go to the road for transportation. This is rather ridiculous, especially when one is sitting in a railroad centre. It increased the cost of transportation, and it is one of the reasons the veneer mill, which was built at considerable expense to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, is very apt to close its doors on a permanent basis. That is how important transportation can be. What factor does it play? Are we in fact given the access to Canadian markets which confederation promised in 1867? The answer is: no, we are not.
Let me take a look at the potato industry. Some hon. members of the House are extremely familiar with the impact of transportation costs on that industry. It hits them in two ways. It hits them on the incoming costs of the requirements of the industry, whether it be fertilizer, machinery or repairs, and the service from that transportation industry is downgraded from what it was 40 years ago. The cost of the production of potatoes has very seriously increased. For instance, the massive increase in fertilizer freight rates had a major impact upon the cost of production.
Historically the soil of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island produced potatoes at a cost which made them competitive even in distant markets. They were competitive with the production of potatoes in central Canada. They were no more than competitive, but they were in the business. The increment in freight costs have been such that they have been removed, to an important degree, from being in a competitive position, in spite of land costs, skills, etc. This is not in conformity with the intention of confederation. Why can we not take a look at that?
March 17, 1981

I submit that the lumber, fishing and agricultural industries have been hurt seriously. If one picks up the paper, one sees where fresh fish marketing is impaired, where CN and CP Express are withdrawing and people are now removed 30, 40 or 50 miles from initial points of delivery of express and LCL freight terminals. This is an inconvenience; this is not the intention of the rail system. If one happens to have drag with a trucking company, one might get a package delivered quickly. But if one does not, and if one required a part in order to repair a piece of machinery in the county of Charlotte or the county of Carleton today, one would get into one's car or half-ton truck and go to Montreal to get it. One does not wait for today's transportation system to make the delivery. This is inconvenience which is certainly not in the best interests of Atlantic Canada or Canada as a whole.
I should like to turn to another item respecting ports. This affects the minister and his bailiwick of Quebec. Today the Government of Canada is dealing with a trade pact in the Pacific rim. It is negotiating a certain agreement that if a ship arrives at a Canadian port as the first port of call, then there will be a certain duty applied to the product being imported into Canada. But, if that ship makes a foreign port of call prior to its port of call in Canada, a higher rate of duty will apply. The Government of Canada is now negotiating to give away the first port of call priority. If this happens, the imports from Australia and New Zealand will probably take place on the Pacific coast or the Atlantic coast of the United States. Those imports will not be handled by our port crews on the east and west coasts of Canada, and, in turn, the exports will probably come down to that ship on one truck with the imports going back on the same truck to their destination in Canada. This represents an intrusion into the market opportunities of Canadian agriculturalists. We are talking of letting food in to take automobile parts out. I am told that is what the deal is all about. Not only will the farmer be hit with lower cost imports, they will be brought in through an American port, rather than Montreal, Saint John, Halifax or Vancouver. This is a very serious threat, not only to the farmer because of the threatened reduction in tariff on imported food, but to the port worker and people all over the country.
It is thoroughly and completely impossible to discuss all the items which need to be discussed with respect to this subject matter as far as Atlantic Canada is concerned. I suggest to the minister we should have a House committee which would have an opportunity to give some serious consideration to the representations of Atlantic Canadian people on behalf of the best interests of Atlantic Canada, its region and the nation of which it is proud. It cannot be done in any other way. How can any group of people properly discuss lumber, potatoes, fish, express, highway, trucking, sea and ports transportation in one day in the House of Commons?
There are people who are studying the problem at the moment. They are prepared to make presentations to the minister. In fact, they are coming to see the minister responsible for DREE, because there are threats to federal investment and to jobs in Atlantic Canada. There is a waste of
Transportation
federal money because of transportation policies which do not add to the developmental opportunities and leadership the government could offer to Atlantic Canada. We need that study in the worst way. I do not know for how long the committee could sit, but it should have the element of time and breadth of interest which would allow it to see what can be done. Can we develop the port, the drydocks, the harbour and shipping in Saint John? What about Halifax harbour, Bel-ledune and Chatham? All these items are of major significance to eastern Canada. They cannot be discussed here, nor can the proper input be made.
I should like to refer to one personal example. Shortly after World War II, I built a little plant. I could not get the necessary machinery in New Brunswick, so I was advised to get it in Montreal or in the west. The reason was that there would be no parts for my machines in New Brunswick; they would have to come from Montreal or perhaps from the west. Up until 1960 to 1965, if a breakdown in the plant occurred, I could phone the supplier of that machinery in order to have that part delivered by rail. If I called as late as five o'clock in the afternoon it would be in my office at one o'clock the next afternoon. But if I owned that plant today and if a machinery breakdown occurred, my only hope of receiving the part in those hours would be to send my own vehicle or a specially-hired vehicle to St. Hyacinthe, Montreal or wherever the point may be, in order to get my plant back into business. I cannot, nor can anyone in New Brunswick, depend upon CP, CN, highway or any other transportation system to deliver as they used to deliver 20, 30 or 40 years ago.
This is what the debate is all about-excessive rates, discrimination against our ports, and failure to keep the agreement of confederation that the markets of Canada should be available at competitive prices to the products of Atlantic Canada. This is what the debate is all about. This is where the government has failed, and it is where maritime members have failed their regions. They will not support Atlantic Canada in an attack on the government to get the things they proclaim they want. We will help them.

I listened with interest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) this afternoon, Mr. Speaker. I believe he is a very humble man, and certainly in terms of transportation policy he has much to be humble about. He is also a decent, philosophical person.
I had intended to speak later tonight, Mr. Speaker; 1 thought I might be the garbageman who would clean up, if I were called upon. What disturbed me most about the summary the Minister of Transport gave of the motion presented by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), was the lack of any zest, energy, enthusiasm, or challenge about something that is of fundamental importance to those of us who are on the periphery, especially those of us from the Atlantic region, from the northern part of the country or from the west.
The motion quite property zeroed in on the problems of Atlantic Canada. I give some credit to the minister and the government, because, after all, no one government has all the answers. As one federal minister of transport said not too long ago, transportation is in a mess. The very structure of our country has been based on transportation. As the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said, perhaps we are overdealing with constitutionalitis to the point that in many areas of endeavour there is a form of governmental constipation because of that constitutionalitis and we are not directing our attention to the many factors and areas in this country which need attention. The government is aware of that; it sets the agenda. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) was government House leader not too long ago and he knows from his experience that the government lays its agenda on the table of this House and the opposition responds to it. If there is a constitutional resolution before the House and the government insists that debate carry on day after day, then naturally it will.
There are other items of importance in the country, however. That is why we in the opposition have taken the opportunity today in this limited type of debate, which fortunately ends in a vote tonight, to focus attention on something that is of fundamental importance. Without getting into the Latin, the reason this is a country from sea to sea is that the CPR formed the western link that made us an entity from sea to sea.
If this matter were not so serious I might use a stronger word than ironic, and say it is rather paradoxical that as we contemplate our navels to determine what we are and where we are going as a nation in terms of the Constitution, the factors that helped make this country great, such as transportation, go for naught. They get shifted aside.
That is what disappointed me when I listened as objectively as I could to the Minister of Transport this afternoon. Point by point he answered the matters raised in the resolution presented by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East. I will not make a rebuttal to his reply because that is not my point at the moment. My point is that I cannot think of any more exhilarating challenge in government than to be minister of
March 17, 1981

transport in the country at this time. Instead of using statistics to show that so many dollars were spent here and some work was done on a seaport there, I had expected something more like a vision. I know the Deputy Prime Minister has heard about visions before, from the late right hon. member for Prince Albert so he may be a little gun-shy of visions. But perhaps we do not talk enough about visions in this House and maybe the night of St. Patrick is not a bad time to talk about them. I do not mean the visions that cause all the problems in Ireland, but rather, visions for this country.
We need a larger vision than was evident in the minister's remarks today. His recital was pedantic, mechanical and, for him, unemotional. Any minister worth his salt, and this minister used to have salt, would get very emotional about this subject.
The minister was right in some of the things he said about Air Canada. We do have different planes now. I can remember, as I am sure the Deputy Prime Minister can, when we used to take the Viscount from the maritimes to Ottawa. The Deputy Prime Minister will remember that to get off the island of Cape Breton, before the causeway was built it was almost necessary to row a boat across the strait to the mainland. Then it took eight or ten hours to fly from Halifax to Ottawa. Now we have the benefits of modern technology and jet planes. Of course, the Minister of Transport does not take credit for all of this. We still cannot fly to New York direct from Ottawa. I am really speaking now about Atlantic area transportation and certainly we can fly much more easily today from Ottawa to Halifax than in the old days. That is to the credit of everyone concerned. But all the problems of this new advancing age have not been solved. The government does not like to admit that there is something called oil and gas. That is dirty stuff developed by these penurious selfish companies which are bleeding Canadian taxpayers to death.
I was very interested this afternoon when the minister rationalized about the icebreaking service and told us to worry about icebreaking on the St. Lawrence and the Gulf because all his experts say the cost of $17 million breaks down to $1.60 per ton and, really, that is not so much. I think the minister should ask his colleagues in cabinet, especially the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), to look into this matter a little further. In that most slanted seven-volume report, published after an eight or ten-year study of the oil and gas industry, there is mention of extra charges over a period of ten-years amounting to $12 billion. Yet apparently the government cannot lay charges against the industry. I am informed by people who know the industry better than I that on the basis of the 35 gallon barrel, taking a ten-year period, the overcharging could be broken down to something like one-third of a cent per gallon.
When the minister tries to rationalize the cost of icebreaking services in the Gulf, I should like him to remember what the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said about the oil companies.
In his own inimitable way the hon. member for Northumb-erland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) justified what the hon.
Transportation
member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) said, that in terms of Atlantic Canada-and hon. members from Atlantic Canada including yourself Mr. Speaker, will appreciate this- unless we become more strongly Atlantic Canadians rather than partisan politicians, some of the basic problems which have existed almost since confederation will not be resolved. The Minister of Transport gave us a recital of statistics this afternoon. To give him his due, certain things have improved but I think he must accept the challenges that lie on the threshold and he must talk about them.
I am not happy to listen to the statistics of the past when 1 know that in the future Dome Petroleum will go offshore to buy the new icebreaking barges to go into the north, and those jobs and that industry will go to Korea or Japan. As an Atlantic Canadian, regardless of how you rationalize it, we thought part of our future was container ports. Almost overnight it is unilaterally being shifted in large measure from Halifax to Montreal. 1 do not have anything against Montreal, but when the history of this time is written, and this comes very close to the background and heritage of the Deputy Prime Minister, it will be said that Atlantic Canadians were not small Canadians when the seaway was to be built. We knew it was in the best interests of the country even though there would be some problems.
Once the decision was made by the government, and it happened to have the same label of government that is now in power, problems started with Sydney Steel. The iron ore came from Sept lies, Ungava and the heartland, and there was not a refitting of the steel mill in Sydney. Some of my predecessors on this side said that was the demarcation of the decline of Sydney Steel. In like fashion we on this side are concerned when we see the Dart Containerline traffic that was supposed to be the base of the new Halifax port activity, unilaterally shifted to Montreal with a tangled corporate web involving Crown corporations and/or federal help in order to keep the St. Lawrence seaway open. That does not make us happy.
When we look to the future there is something else we talk about in this House. The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance was supposed to help with the financing, but so far there has been no commitment whatsoever in terms of the future of Atlantic Canada. I refer to the pipeline extension east of Quebec City. This will come back to haunt the Minister of Finance. It will come back to haunt the Minister of Finance that Atlantic Canadians did not have the opportunity to make a bid on the LNG project between Gros Cacouna and the Strait of Canso, in the backyard of the Minister of Finance. It does not give us much hope for the future when the Minister of Finance is not prepared to exercise the weight of his office to get the National Energy Board to move on the whole operation. The Minister of Finance can smile, but I suggest it will be the smile of the proverbial cat that gave you parliamentary indigestion.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly felt there could have been a few more minutes to wrap it all up, but it has been a very interesting evening so far, and I guess some of the very interesting comments were made by the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne). I particularly noted his comment on patronage, and from his remarks tonight I was very optimistic that recognition might be the first step to a cure.
There were comments tonight on the committee system as an appropriate method of dealing with transportation issues. I think a great many people in this House are finding that the committee system is not an effective way to deal with some of the problems that face this nation, particularly with the spending of billions of dollars in departmental estimates, or even in dealing with programs-some certainly have more success than others. I think by and large, however, with some of the reforms of the committee system suggested we may see a better transportation system in the country. I think there is an even greater potential for reform. In watching passage of this
March 17, 1981

particular motion through the House tonight, I think the whole question of how we approach opposition days may be worth looking at.
The motion before us starts out by condemning the government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), and then itemizes some very serious concerns affecting everyone in this House. I have spoken to government members, members of the official opposition and our own party who are concerned about many of the items. Unfortunately these motions are always condemned to defeat in advance. There are positive statements in this motion, but they are couched in such a way it can never succeed. That is unfortunate because I think some of the government members recognize many of the problems, and support some of the suggested solutions.
Although I suppose we are going to support this motion, I am reluctant to join in condemning the Minister of Transport.
1 may have felt a little differently early in my term, but I have found he is a person who is at least open and willing to discuss problems, in some cases more so than other members of the government. I certainly appreciate some of the things he has done there.
The point I am making is we had a very interesting debate on El Salvador and Central America Monday last, and 1 think many members of the official opposition, although they had difficulty supporting the motion the way it was drafted, supported the concept. I guess I am saying the same thing tonight.
I wish the motion was couched in such a way that a positive outcome was possible with regard to the common problems we recognize.
With those comments I should like to move on to one aspect of transportation that concerns me, an aspect I think it is of vital concern to all Canadians.
I have spoken on this many times in the House and I know many others are vitally concerned with it. I refer to the whole area of marine transportation. Many people in this House recognize that the Department of Transport is a monster, containing as it does the air, marine and surface administrations. Basically it is so vital and so large there is a feeling that the department should be divided. On a number of occasions I have placed a number of questions and suggestions on the order paper that we appoint a minister of marine transportation. The other day in response to a question the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he would give that concept consideration. I would like to make some arguments this evening as to why that should be done and done very quickly.
The issue of a Canadian merchant fleet has been debated many times in this House. Many members of the government, the loyal opposition, and the New Democratic Party, have on many occasions indicated support for this. If we look back we will see that Canada is about the tenth largest trading nation in the world. The goods we exported and imported in 1979 amounted to about $38 billion, of which 10 per cent, roughly $4 billion, can be related to the freight bill. In coming years we will be looking at increasing wheat shipments, but as the world converts from more expensive petroleum fuels to coal, we are going to see a massive development of marine transportation to
Transportation
haul that coal to those nations short of it from those that have it in abundance. Ports will have to be developed and, in short, billions and billions of dollars will have to be spent on marine transportation development.
After the world coal report was produced someone made the statement that there were not enough shipyards in the world to build quickly enough the vessels required to carry the volume of coal when we really begin to make that conversion by the end of the century. A Canadian merchant fleet is going to be a very important aspect of our marine transportation system. It is going to provide jobs for Canadians through crewing these vessels, jobs in building them and in allied industries, and it is going to place in Canada a technology that will, if we take the opportunity, make us world traders in ships and marine facilities. Basically what we have to do is look seriously at bringing a Canadian merchant fleet onstream very soon.
It is interesting to note the arguments, and there have been ten to 20 years of studies, as to why we do not have a merchant fleet. The government's policy for years has been that there is a large pool of surplus shipping in the world; it provides a cheap source of transport for Canadian goods on these flags of convenience ships using cheap labour, with very low safety standards and a variety of other cost-cutting methods, and that it has been a boon to Canada in supplying cheap transportation. However, I would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is a hook in that and a very dangerous one. Shipyards in Canada are no longer capable, I would suggest, of building the kinds of vessels that would put Canada out front in carrying her own resources around the world, or at least a share of those resources. The capability is not there and what we have done by this very pennywise and pound foolish policy is place ourselves in very great jeopardy for the next few decades; maybe forever. I suggest, therefore, it is unfortunate that the resolution tonight was not couched in such a way as to make a positive statement about the development of a Canadian merchant fleet.
Another aspect of this suggestion about the appointment of a minister for marine transportation, given the task of developing a marine force for Canada and co-ordinating the efforts of government and industry to bring about this marine strategy in a way that would provide maximum benefits for Canada, is the business of offshore and Arctic development. The oil companies are now coming before the national resources and public works committee talking about their plans in the Canada lands area of Hibernia, off Sable Island, the Labrador shelf, the Beaufort Sea and the Arctic islands, and they are using some interesting figures. Dome talks about spending $40 billion on platforms for exploration, production and transportation of supplies in and the resource out. Mobil Oil was talking the other day about their activities off the east coast and it presented some rough and dirty figures. It was talking about $5 billion for marine platforms. Mobil is working with semisubmersible rigs and developing platforms to work on the sea bottom. When Mobil get into production they plan to spend roughly $5 billion over the next decade.

March 17, 1981
Transportation
With respect to the offshore role of Gulf Resources of Canada, Gulf officials spoke the other day about approximately $5 billion for marine platforms. Gulf had not yet decided on technology; whether it would dredge up islands and plant their production facilities on those islands or go with more conventional marine platforms. However, they spoke about a quick $5 billion figure.
Officials of PanArctic Resources were here today. They are working in a number of areas, some of them on land. They are beginning to work offshore in very deep waters. One particular oil strike was at 1,100 feet. With respect to the projects in which PanArctic is involved with other companies, they are talking about $40 billion to $50 billion. This is projected between now and the 1990s. Some things are on the drawing board; some things are a reality. Dome Petroleum is considering delivering gas to Japan by 1986. It is considering delivering gas out of the Arctic pilot project by 1985. That is just a very short few years away.
The oil companies to which I have referred were asked what impediments they see to Canadians participating in building platforms for exploration, for production and for transportation. Every one of them indicated that there is a serious problem. First, the resource industry, government and the manufacturing industry which will be involved in providing maximization of benefits for Canadians, are not talking on a formal, regular basis to see that those works come to Canadian shipyards and allied industries. That is the first problem.
There seems to be a problem within the government itself. Various government departments seem to be developing a fragmented approach or are actually working at times at cross purposes. When there is an order of roughly $60 billion to $100 billion, we as Canadians cannot afford that kind of impediment.
The other impediment is that Canadian shipyards are not in a position to deliver. Let us go back for a moment to the case of Mobil Oil. Mobil went offshore for a drilling rig. It went to Canadian shipyards and said, "Can you build it?" Those shipyards said, "Sorry, we cannot; we are not set up to do it". A specific delivery date was specified, and Canadian shipyards could not do it. Work valued at $300 million went offshore.
Dome Petroleum entered into an agreement just a week and a half or two weeks ago. Dome Petroleum wants to spend $200 million on a barge. The barge is to be a floating drydock to work in the Arctic. Dome went to every Canadian shipyard and asked if this barge it wanted, made from 7,500 tons of steel, could be built in Canada. That would have been a very large project. Roughly 150 to 200 jobs would have been involved. Every Canadian shipyard was asked if there could be a delivery by June 1 because the Arctic window opens for only a short period of time. It is only open from roughly July 15 to September 15. If the barge does not go in then, it must wait a year. Some projects tie up $1 million a day for a year, and that money cannot be wasted. The Canadian shipyards invited to participate were asked for a June 1 delivery date. None of them could meet that date. Dome went offshore and found
that no foreign supplier could do it, so the date was moved to September 1. Canadian shipbuilders still could not meet the date, but one offshore shipyard could. That barge is now being built in Japan.
Dome had the same problem with supply vessels for the Beaufort Sea. They are built in Louisiana. Apparently they have a very special design. There now is a need to acquire an icebreaking tug; a very large and powerful machine. This is on the drawing board. Strengthened hulls and huge motors are required, but delivering the motors at the time the hulls are built will require a two-year delay. This equipment is needed in the Arctic when the window is open. If Canadians cannot build it, that tug will be built offshore.
The moral of the story is that resource companies are not talking seriously enough with the shipbuilding companies. Government is not giving adequate or co-ordinated attention to the development of Canadian shipyards. Government is not facilitating developments in the Arctic.
Perhaps a way out of this particular dilemma would be to appoint a minister of marine transportation and to give such minister the task of developing a marine industrial strategy which would have the resources to co-ordinate and make sure that Canadians cash in as much as possible on that $60 billion to $100 billion Arctic development.
Who knows what merchant fleet development there might be when we start moving large quantities of coal out of this country? But without the necessary co-ordination many of these developments will go offshore. We will be supplying only the nuts and bolts for these massive platforms being built offshore.
There are other aspects of this which seem somewhat strange to someone standing outside and watching. It must certainly seem strange to some government members that the government uses a large number of marine platforms. The government spends a tremendous amount of money. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans is spending roughly $90 million on a new fishing vessel acquisition program. The RCMP has a fleet of vessels it uses in the delivery of law enforcement services at sea. The Department of Transport provides search and rescue services through the coastguard as well as icebreaking services and a host of other things. That department has a very large fleet. The Department of National Defence is developing a new frigate program as well as a destroyer life extension program.
From the information we have it appears to someone from the outside that there is a great deal of fragmentation in the way we are obtaining marine platforms. Each department has its own vessels. Each is building its own empire. This has created a great deal of fragmentation.
It strikes me that if the government is building all those vessels, whether they be new frigates for the armed forces, whether they be under a destroyer life extension program, whether they be fisheries vessels or RCMP vessels or whether money is spent on coastguard repair work or new construction, it should all be co-ordinated, not by way of awarding contracts
March 17, 1981

to the lowest bidders, but through the development and enhancement of a Canadian marine industrial strategy.
Bill C-48 really is not strong enough to demand Canadian content, but subsidization and tax programs should all be brought together under a minister of marine transportation in order to create a marine industrial strategy for Canadians. This would be a tremendous project, and there is tremendous potential. That makes a great deal of sense to me and to many with whom I have spoken. We should not fail to do this. Mobil has already done it, Dome has already done it and every shipping company listed here and every carrier has done it.
I would like to run through some figures. They are not particularly important, but in 1976 roughly 100,000 tonnes of Canadian shipping were built offshore. In 1977, 164,000 tonnes were built offshore. In 1978, 67,000 tonnes were built offshore. In short, a tremendous amount of our shipping capability is being lost to other countries. Many of these ships are registered in other countries, and repaired in other countries.
I have dealt with our opportunities in the Arctic. I have dealt with the problems faced by companies which want to build their vessels in Canada. They cannot get Canadian shipyards to handle the work, so other countries are providing their ships. In the Arctic the Offshore Supply Association- which is a wholly-owned subsidiary of a German company, Preussag of Bremen-intends to register six of its 92 vessels in Canada so that they can work in the Arctic. I submit that those should not be supplied from West Germany, with returns going back to West Germany. Those vessels should be produced by Canadians in Canadian shipyards supplied by many other Canadian allied industries. This would provide an additional benefit.
I would like to complete my contribution to this debate tonight. I strongly suggest to the Minister of Transport and members of the government who are vitally concerned about this, whether they be from Atlantic Canada, from Quebec, from Sorel, from Levis or from Montreal, that we need a minister of marine transportation. We need a marine industrial strategy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO DEAL ADEQUATELY WITH NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by saying how delighted I am to participate in this debate on a motion moved by the Progressive Conservative Party which calls on this House to condemn the failure of the government to deal adequately with national transportation problems. In our motion, we condemn my good friend, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), in particular, for:
1.	abandoning the use of transportation as a tool of national and regional
economic development;
2.	allowing Canadian National Railways to totally disregard legitimate maritime business needs and close CN Express offices without adequate financial
justification-
Transportation
7. failing to bring before the House acceptable legislation dealing with a new national transportation act, ports policy, the maritime code, or coastal shipping;
There a. e other grievances.
My colleagues have contributed usefully to this debate on a variety of subjects. I am particularly glad my colleague from Prince Edward Island, the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass), has been able to participate and to deal with a number of issues of special import to my province and to the region in general.
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I intend to focus almost exclusively on rail transportation, including all the various operations of Canadian National. I do so, not because I think air transport, shipping or highways are not important-in fact they are-but I think by concentrating on rail transportation I will be able to illustrate more clearly than in any other fashion two broad points. The first is that the government is almost totally insensitive to the problems and concerns of the Atlantic provinces, and the second is that the government is especially unaware of the importance of transportation to the economy of the region and to the quality of life there.
It must be remembered that the Atlantic provinces were not always poor, disadvantaged and destitute. At the time of confederation we were a fairly prosperous region. We were approaching a degree of self-sufficiency with strong trade ties, for example, with the northeastern tier states of our southern neighbours. In the 1860s, our region had a well-developed maritime shipping industry. Ours ranked fourth among the great merchant marines of the world, and this sort of enterprise spawned all kinds of industries beyond those particular ones, including a significant financial system which included about a dozen banks, two of which were the most substantial and stable in all of North America, not to mention insurance and marine companies.
Soon after confederation the situation turned dramatically for the worse. I would be the last member of the House to argue that confederation has not been good for the Atlantic provinces or for my province in particular. That is not the point of my message. I am saying, however, that despite many social and economic benefits from confederation, the policies of successive federal governments, particularly Liberal governments, consciously or subconsciously have favoured other regions of Canada at the expense of our own, especially central Canada. I might mention, for instance, the fact that high tariffs have consistently favoured the industrial heartland of the country, southern Quebec and Ontario, a policy which, whatever its merits in terms of developing the national economy as an independent force, involved the Atlantic region paying a very high price indeed. The national policy, as it was called, was begun in the early part of our history and was followed to the present. It is not an isolated example.
Nowhere is such a bias in favour of the central part of the country more true than in transportation. 1 think in that regard a historical perspective is vital to an understanding of the importance of transportation to the region and of the failure of national transportation policies to serve the region.

March 17, 1981
Transportation
1 want to skim over the history very briefly. But in doing so I stress, in particular, that Prince Edward Island entered confederation because of the firm commitment made by Canada-as it then was-to complete the P.E.I. railroad and to maintain it forever and a day. I have in front of me the Terms of Union between Prince Edward Island and the rest of Canada. They stress:
Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the Island and the mainland of the Dominion, winter and summer, thus placing the Island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial Railway and the railway system of the Dominion.
That was a firm commitment by Canada to provide P.E.I. with continuous rail service-not only to complete the P.E.I. railway but to maintain it. It was an article of faith as far as Islanders were concerned. The continued existence of the railway was something akin to an inalienable right.
After the P.E.I. railway was completed and, eventually, after the Intercolonial Railway in the Atlantic region was completed in the 1870s, the two railways were meshed and incorporated into the Canadian National Railways system around 1919. But, even though changes were made to the specifics of the arrangements so far as the railways were concerned, the fact remains that the commitment continues to this very day.
It is interesting to note that in August, 1973, there was a strike on Prince Edward Island in CN marine service, which effectively cut P.E.I. off from the rest of Canada for a period of time, to the great detriment of the local economy. P.E.I. then took the federal government to court, even as far as the Supreme Court of Canada, because it considered that strike to be a breach of the Terms of Union of Prince Edward Island in confederation. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that P.E.I. won its case, which further confirms the very strong commitment the federal government has to our island province to maintain the railway connection. That commitment extends to the region as a whole, because the Intercolonial Railway was completed as a term of entry for the other maritime provinces into confederation. It was part of their confederation bargain. The Intercolonial was not set up as a profit-making enterprise; it was set up for the better interests of the region as a whole, even though that particular facility might incur a loss.
When the Canadian National Railways took over the Intercolonial Railway, as it did other parts of the railway system in Canada, to provide a country-wide system, such a commitment to continue railway service-and a minimal service at that, below which the region would not be allowed to fall-has never, so far as the courts have been concerned, been removed. The commitment continues to the present.
1 want to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that while this commitment stands, the federal government, almost since the time of the collapse of the Intercolonial Railway-or since its absorbtion by CN-has pursued a steady, programmed effort to downgrade the railway throughout the Atlantic region. The most recent example, of course, is Canadian National Express. I want to dwell on it for a couple of minutes, by way of illustration only.
My colleagues have demonstrated very adequately this afternoon and evening the importance of that vital service. It is important to business people, to farmers, to fishermen and, indeed, to the general public. It is an essential tool of commerce for the whole area. I am talking about the general field of small parcel delivery and service.
In 1976 there were 19 CN Express terminals in the mari-times. That figure was later reduced to 15. In 1981 there was a plan to slash the number to five, a reduction of something like 76 per cent. At one point Prince Edward Island was to be denied locally-supplied CN service; to the extent it would be allowed to continue, the whole shebang was to be turned over to profit-oriented trucking companies. E cannot stress strongly enough the inadequacy of such an arrangement.
I have nothing against trucking companies, but I regret very much that the trucking companies which would have taken over this service on P.E.I. were off-island. Trucking companies, just as with any other profit-oriented enterprise, are not designed essentially to provide a public service in the way CN was set up to do. If the express service were turned over to trucking companies it would be reduced and provided on the terms of the trucking companies which are not always in the public interest. Trucking companies do not have a national network such as CN's. They are profit-oriented and do not have a public mandate as CN does. Nor do they have the expertise to assist their patrons, the people who use express service, with packaging, advice on the proper mode of transport, or the identification of individual parcels which are lost. Trucking companies do not have that expertise, and they have no particular interest in developing it. Moreover, when two or three carriers get into the act, add-on charges are involved. So, the eventual cost to consumers would be very much higher than if the existing CN service were continued.
Largely because of pressure from myself, the government of Prince Edward Island, the CN employees involved and the public at large, the minister undertook to be in touch with Dr. Bandeen, the president of Canadian National, to have Prince Edward Island exempted from the scheduled ten CN Express office closures. I welcome that and congratulate the minister for taking the initiative. But the fact remains that the number of employees has been reduced from 41 to 19, and the service has been substantially truncated. It will be basically restricted to within Charlottetown, and between Charlottetown and other off-island centres. Most of the connections between Charlottetown and other communities within the island will be severed. Apparently the figure of 19 employees includes one manager, but that was not my understanding of the commitment that CN Express would maintain 19 full-time employees on P.E.I. In addition, CN officials, perhaps unbeknownst to the minister, have been fiddling with the numbers to the extent of threatening to keep only 11, 12 or 13 full-time employees, with the others only on a part-time or relief basis, to be called into service at the discretion of CN.
March 17, 1981

I know the minister would not breach the commitment he gave in the House on February 4 and February 24 to maintain CN Express services on the island at 19 full-time employees, or in that vicinity. I will hold him to his commitment. I am sure, because he is an honourable man, that he will live up to it. Also, I congratulate him for keeping the Sydney office open on the grounds that that particular community is in a low employment area and thus needs special consideration.
In my remaining minutes, I want to stress that the CN Express situation is only an illustration. I appreciate the argument made sometimes by CN that it was losing money with the service, something like $50 million in 1979. But one wonders how hard CN tried to turn a profit. I suspect it did the same thing with CN Express as it did with CN passenger service. The company created a situation which caused people not to use the service, so that it could use the non-use of the service as a rationale for abolishing it, when the real reason had nothing to do with whether or not the service was being used by the public. I find it hard to believe that CN cannot compete with private couriers and similar specialized operaiors who are often proceeding on a shoestring. In any event, the CN Express on P.E.I. was operating at near-peak capacity. I am told by people who have looked very closely at the figures that over a period of time the CN Express terminal on Prince Edward Island consistently operated at 95 per cent capacity, by CN's own standards. It is, therefore, beyond my understanding how CN could threaten to abolish that service on the grounds that it was being underused.
The profit of Canadian National Railways in 1979 was $208 million, up $72.1 million from 1978. It is clear that CN is hell-bent on making a profit at the expense of providing services, at the expense of its public mandate, and at the expense of the terms of entry into confederation by Prince Edward Island and the other Atlantic provinces. It is operating like a private corporation. It is no different from Canadan Pacific or, for that matter, Eastern Provincial Airways. It has set upon a course which emphasizes consolidation, bigness and concentrating on key market centres, major metropolitan market centres such as Montreal and Toronto. By definition that almost excludes the Atlantic provinces. This emphasis will have various consequences in terms of our prospects for regional development and alleviating the economic disparities we suffer.
Other examples could be cited of the steady withdrawal of Canadian National from the Atlantic region. In Prince Edward Island there was the removal of passenger service; the efforts of CN, some of them successful, to abandon important rail lines; and the threat to the carload centre, the major office for the movement of heavy freight to and from the province and within it. Most recently there was the threat to the rail car service centre which provides emergency and routine services to 7he cars; it has been moved practically holus-bolus to another, off-island centre. Finally there is the example of CN Express cited earlier. They are all part of a pattern of programmed erosion of the operations of Canadian National on Prince Edward Island.
Transportation
This is most regrettable. The P.E.I, case parallels other horror stories to which some of my colleagues have addressed themselves; including the downplaying of the Halifax harbour and in particular the Dart Containerline crisis in Halifax. It is a truly tragic situation to which Canadian National is a party.
We must appreciate that transportation is not a luxury. It is not only important; it is essential to the region. It is a vital tool for economic development. We in the Atlantic region have particular requirements by virtue of the fact that we are far from our markets and are also often far from our sources of supply. We need in Canada a total look at the federal government's plans for transportation in the region over the next five years. In particular we must look at the special role of Canadian National in those plans. We must look at the role of air and other modes of transportation in that over-all scheme. It is because the federal government has failed miserably to sustain a regionally-sensitive transportation policy that I call upon all members of the House to condemn the government and the record of the Minister of Transport. The government does not appreciate the objectives of a regionally-sensitive transportation policy, the realization of which was one of the terms of entry into confederation by the maritime provinces.

Transportation
